subsubtopic: VOLCANIC ASH FALL-OUT FROM ERUPTION OF MOUNT ST. HELENS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
The recent eruption of Mount St. Helens in the state of Washington has caused severe human tragedy as well as extensive property damage. The volcanic ash fall-out from the eruption is extensive, affecting large areas of the United States of America and Canada, with as yet undetermined short and long-term effects. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone):
That this House direct the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment to undertake immediately an environmental assessment of the volcanic ash fall-out on human health, as well as the possible effects on wildlife, turbidity and acidity effects on lakes, stream and soils in affected areas of western Canada; and, furthermore, that the government report to this House on this matter without delay.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Given the fact that the Liberal government in March, 1978, brought in the Canadian Human Rights Act and established the Human Rights Commission, given that we all should fully endorse the principle of equal pay for work of equal value, and in view of the fact that recently the Human Rights Commission investigators have found that about 3,000 low-paid public servants-most of whom are women-employed as food service workers, laundry workers and miscellaneous services such as gatekeepers, are not receiving equal pay for work of equal value, even though their work is classified as equal in value by the government, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith):
That this government move immediately to correct the discrimination in wages found by the Human Rights Commission with respect to these 3,000 low-paid service workers, and to uphold the principle of equal pay for work of equal value.

Madam Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. Since income that would have been available through Conservative party energy pricing policies in Canada is not now available to the federal government, and because increased federal income through energy pricing contemplated now might be completely lost to subsidization payments for expensive imported oil, can the Prime Minister please tell the House how, or if, the government will provide, for the sake of self-sufficiency, the $100 billion funding necessary to develop non-conventional and alternate energy resources in Canada?

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FORCES IN COMBATING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. At present, there are over 230 forest fires still burning in the three prairie provinces, as well as many more in northwestern Ontario and British Columbia, as a result of prolonged hot, dry weather. Thousands of lives are endangered by these fires; indeed, at least two communities have already been evacuated.
Will the minister put at the disposal of civilian fire-fighting authorities all available armed forces equipment and personnel in order to help ease this very serious situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FORCES IN COMBATING
speechtext:
1 can assure the hon. member, through you, Madam Speaker, that the armed forces are at the service of the civilian population wherever they are. At the request of the Saskatchewan government, we have provided a squadron of aircraft to check on these fires and to help transport people who are fighting them. We already have two helicopters in northern Ontario, two in Saskatchewan, and two Hercules aircraft helping people wherever help is needed. The hon. member can be assured that the armed forces are at the service of the Canadian people all the time, wherever they are needed.
May 22, 1980

subsubtopic: OIL EXPLORATION IN BEAUFORT SEA-DANGER OF SPILLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In response to questioning on Tuesday, the minister stated that the report of the Arctic Waters Advisory Committee on drilling in the Beaufort Sea was thoroughly reviewed by himself and his department. This report stated that the government "is not and will not be prepared to make important decisions which will be required in the future if drilling activities continue."
Rather than give what I would call blind assurances that there are no risks involved in this drilling activity, will the minister explain what plans he has to improve the government's capability to respond to the environmental risks associated with increased drilling activity in these Arctic waters?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: OIL EXPLORATION IN BEAUFORT SEA-DANGER OF SPILLS
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, I would advise the hon. member that his leader asked questions on this subject earlier in the week or in the latter part of last week. There is a contingency plan with respect to drilling activities. If there should be any mishap at all-and, as I say, the possibility is very minimal indeed, according to all the expert advice I have received-we have a contingency plan. 1 am prepared to talk about that contingency plan in the standing committee this evening. We shall no doubt go into that matter.

subsubtopic: OIL EXPLORATION IN BEAUFORT SEA-DANGER OF SPILLS
speechtext:
Also on Tuesday last, the minister referred to advances in technology in connection with drilling in the north. May I say that these have to do only with drilling in the north, not with environmental preservation and protection. He further referred to safeguards with respect to relief well-drilling this season, no doubt in regard to the September 25 deadline for the termination of all drilling activities.
Will he assure the House that in no circumstances will any drilling or production testing be allowed after this date, as happened last year, regardless of pressure from Dome or any other company active in the Beaufort Sea?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: OIL EXPLORATION IN BEAUFORT SEA-DANGER OF SPILLS
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that neither I nor the government will, under any circumstances, make a decision based on pressure from Dome or anybody else. The fact is that there is a 20-day grace period
Oral Questions
after September 20 which could be used for continued drilling, if all the advice we have with respect to weather conditions and all other risks which might be involved is positive in the sense that there is very little, if any, risk at all in continued drilling during that grace period. It will be judged solely on the basis of that expert advice. If the advice indicates drilling is not warranted, we shall adhere to the deadline.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
My question, Madam Speaker, is addressed to the Prime Minister, who earlier in the question period agreed with the Minister of Finance that the policy of the government is to phase out or do away with the oil import compensation program.
Will the Prime Minister explain what the time-frame is for that operation, because the last figure we have is $3.1 billion, a cost which is going to increase now because of recent increases in the price of oil? Is it to be phased out this year? Where will the amount in excess of the $3.1 billion come from? Where does he propose to get it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in answer to a previous question, I indicated that it would be done over a period of time. Therefore, the answer to the part of the question related to this year is "No". But the hon. member must understand the policy put forward by the government. It is a policy of blended prices and, naturally, we would have to continue to pay the international price for imported oil. But we will pay less for the oil.
When?
Even the hon. member from Kingston will understand that they are not going to accept lower prices for our imported oil.
Oh, oh!

Also, if she had been more attentive to the policy which was stated by the minister and various members of this government, she would understand that the blended price means we are going to pay the international price for the imported oil and that we will pay less than the international price for Canadian oil. The result will be a blended price.

We all realize that this is a blended government, or a blanded government, but even a blended government cannot perform miracles. The Prime Minister said, on CBC radio on February 10:
We obviously would have to subsidize the price of imported oil. We would continue to do this as we did in the seventies.
This was a pledge to the Canadian people, before the election of February 18, that he would continue to subsidize the price of imported oil. Today he tells us he is not going to

OraI Questions
continue to subsidize the price of imported oil. You are not Mandrake the Magician. You cannot fool the Canadian people indefinitely with blended prices on blended prices and blanded prices. How long will this commitment last? The Prime Minister implied that all during the eighties he would subsidize the price of imported oil as he did in the seventies. Is he now doing away with that commitment, as he has done away with so many others?

Madam Speaker, the element of cross-subsidization which we began in 1974 will, indeed, disappear as soon as the blended price is in. We will pay to foreigners the international price, and the price in Canada will be a lesser price.
Where will the money come from?
What Canadians will pay will be a composite of those two prices.

Madam Speaker, a supplementary on behalf of simple, uncomplicated Canadians like myself who cannot understand this new algebra or new mathematics. There are $3.1 billion which the government admits it is going to cost for oil import subsidies this year. How is the Prime Minister going to replace all, or part, of that? Who is going to pay to make that up? The taxpayers will subsidize it, the $3.1 billion, under the present program, but that is going to change with the blended program.
Who, then, is going to pick up the money that is saved under $3.1 billion? It is the Canadian people, is it not, and therefore the government will not have to subsidize because they are going to collect it from the Canadian people-from taxes on heating oil and taxes on all oil products, another sleight-of-hand, gerrymandering that is planned?
I understand the hon. member is making a suggestion. I will have the minister look into it.

speechtext:

May 22, 1980

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: BUDGET FOR 1980-81
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I must inform the hon. member for Victoria that over the last five years the average increase in the defence budget has been about 3 per cent and that we plan on having the same figure for 1980-81. The present budget or, if you prefer, the current estimates indicate a similar rate, namely, an increase of 3 per cent in real value.

subsubtopic: BUDGET FOR 1980-81
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that the minister's parliamentary secretary is much more forthcoming and straightforward in her answers to questions.
Could the minister tell the House if he was briefed, either before he went to Brussels or while at that meeting, on the cost overrun of the Airborne Early Warning system, whose costs seem now to have got out of hand?
Can the minister tell the House what action he took, as the minister representing the Canadian government, to enforce appropriate cost controls for that program so that Canada is not liable to pay a fixed percentage of unlimited costs for the new AEW system?

subsubtopic: BUDGET FOR 1980-81
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not aware of any program or measure taken by the Department of National Defence which is not controlled at budget level. At times it can happen that these costs will increase due to inflation or certain circumstances beyond our control, but the budget as a whole is very well controlled. When certain expenses increase in an uncontrollable manner it is because we do not have any control over inflation or it is due to some other factors.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 wonder if I might ask the government House leader if he could inform the House of his plans for tomorrow and into next week. I understand he is prepared to designate next Friday as an allotted day for the opposition. Could he confirm that for me, please?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to confirm that next Friday will be an allotted day. The business for tomorrow will be the Federal Business Development Bank Act and the Bret-ton Woods Agreements Act, on both of which we hope to be able to complete second reading stage.

As for the events of next Monday, Madam Speaker, there is a change which is important to note, namely that the president of Mexico is going to speak in the House, not at 11 a.m. but at 2.15 p.m., contrary to what may have been announced by some

media. The oral question period will be at 4.30 on the same day, and after that we shall pursue consideration of the old age security bill, to grant senior citizens an increase of $35 in their guaranteed income supplement.
After this bill is passed we intend to begin consideration of another piece of legislation to provide government with supplementary borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1980-81, namely Bill C-30. If before next Friday, which is an allotted day, an opposition day, as I have just mentioned, if we have enough time we hope to be able to complete the study of Bills C-19, C-28, C-3 or of motion No. 1 in the name of the government.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, on a number of occasions I have asked the minister whether he would be prepared to make the appropriate reference to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence so that there could be reports by parliamentary delegations to that committee, which is something which has been done before. I have indicated that we would be prepared to do that without debate. Is the government House leader prepared to make an announcement today as to whether that is appropriate, and could he put the appropriate order on the order paper so that we could proceed?

speechtext: The appropriate notice will be given no later than today, so that we hope to be in a position to adopt the motion tomorrow or at the latest at the beginning of next week.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is one other matter which concerns the House of Commons. There was some discussion during the period of time that the committee on televising the proceedings of the House of Commons was in existence, that committee being under Mr. Speaker Jerome. That committee does not exist at the moment, but that discussion ranged around the possibility of engaging in a pilot program to televise the work of standing committees of the House of Commons. There had been some discussions about that. The discussions did not lead to any final conclusion.
1 am not assessing blame when 1 raise that matter-not by any means-but would the government House leader give consideration to arranging for the television of a standing committee of the House of Commons or at least equipping one room on a temporary basis, or whichever would be the least expensive, for televising the work of committees so that we can have a pilot project on that? 1 think that if that does not happen, there is a great part of the work of the House of Commons which would not be seen. I understand there is space available now through satellite transmission to carry the televising of the committees of the House of Commons. There is a considerable amount of space and time available. If the government House leader would consider that, I would be
Business of the House
grateful. When he is considering it, could he tell the House whether he has any feeling about reconstituting that committee on televising the House of Commons under the chairmanship of the Speaker of the House of Commons, as was the case in other parliaments?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague will recall that a few months, or rather a few years ago, it was our government which decided to bring Parliament closer to the people by televising the debates of the House. A committee was established at the time to launch this experiment which has now proven successful, and it was in this spirit that a committee of the House was appointed by the Speaker to ensure that the systems then being tested would bring about the results that we have today, that is that the debates would be televised according to the concept of the electronic Hansard.
Now, Madam Speaker, the suggestion concerning the committees deserves consideration. However, I must say to my hon. colleague that televising the debates of the House has made us realize that certain procedures are outmoded, and it is important to consider the fact that there is room for improving many elements of the procedures of the House.
While respecting the spirit of Parliament, we should modernize it. We can also make it more effective and more human.
I would not want to be so narrow-minded as to limit the experiment of television to a single committee. I believe that in the next few months, in consultation with all hon. members, we must try to bring about a reform through which we shall be able once again to show to the public now watching us in the House of Commons through television that we can be effective while respecting the rights of the opposition and that we are also able to adjust ourselves to the requirements of the eighties.
All these changes, all these modifications, all these reforms should be discussed by representatives of all parties, and I do not think that it would be wise at this stage to launch a very limited experiment, at least not before the summer recess in order to televise the proceedings of a single committee.
If my learned colleague wants to think about reform proposals, I know that he has already submitted a project containing some good ideas, such as shortening the length of speeches at second reading, which I would gladly support. Certain other changes seemed less acceptable to my mind. In any case, we are open to discussion, and I invite all members who have constructive suggestions to make to do so as soon as possible so that we may, to the great satisfaction of the Canadian public, and of course of parliamentarians, make Parliament even more interesting than it is now.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which arose out of statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in this House on May 14. After my quick lesson yesterday, Madam Speaker, I should like to start again and quote from the middle of the paragraph on page 1061 of Hansard for that day, where the minister said:
-to ask the local population and community to react to financial barriers being imposed when they should not be imposed in the light of the huge payments being made by taxpayers in all of Canada for medicare in Alberta, as everywhere else-though not in Saskatchewan, by the way.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister that over the last number of years the taxpayers of Canada have contributed to medicare in Saskatchewan in 1977-78 to the tune of $193.5 million, in 1978-79 to the tune of $225.9 million. I am pointing that out because perhaps the minister has not paid attention to the province of Saskatchewan and does not feel that the rest of the taxpayers of Canada are contributing to health care in that province.
May 22, 1980

1 should like to point out to the minister that up to 30 per cent of the doctors in the province of Saskatchewan are billing their patients directly. This has continued for the last two to three years. I should like to point out the actions taken by the government in Saskatchewan to rectify this practice which members of the NDP and some other members in the House find reprehensible. What the province of Saskatchewan has done is to introduce a bill in 1979 to amend the Saskatchewan medicare insurance act to require physicians to provide patients with information on how to receive reimbursement from the provincial insurance commission. This is not a great deal of help to people who will suffer a financial loss of probably 80 per cent.
in closing, let me state briefly that at present Saskatchewan is suffering along with other provinces from direct billing by physicians. 1 hope it is the minister's responsibility to rectify this problem.
If you find this to be a question of privilege, Madam Speaker, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), that the Minister of National Health and Welfare recognize that the people of Canada contribute to medicare in the province of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. 1 have to rule on this question of privilege. I think the hon. member is expecting me to tell him that he has no question of privilege. Obviously this is a dispute arising between two members where interpretation of what was said is not agreed upon.
I think the time has come for me to read to members instances where, a question of privilege does apply, because it seems to me that members are bringing up questions of privilege quite often. Of course, the Chair encourages members to bring up questions of privilege when they are quite sure that there is a privilege involved, but I think I have had to rule sufficiently often on questions of privilege which were simply disputes between two members. Members should try to be a little bit more mindful of the reasons for which one can invoke a question of privilege, and I will read the reasons to members.
1 should like to refer to Beauchesne's fifth edition, which reads as follows:
A dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
The failure of a minister of the Crown to answer a question may not be raised as a question of privilege.
Statements made outside the House by a member may not be used as the base for a question of privilege.
Many matters, such as the absence of a minister of the Crown from a committee studying his estimates, may constitute a grievance but not a question of privilege.
Even that is quite a serious matter. In this particular case the member is raising a question of privilege based on remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on May 14. He is raising that point today, on May 22. Beauchesne's fifth edition also indicates the following:
A question of privilege must be brought to the attention of the House at the first possible opportunity.
There was ample opportunity for the member to bring up this question of privilege. The member was in the House. I do not know if he was in the House the day after the minister made this statement, but he was in the House several times since that time. It seems to me that several days have passed during which time the hon. member did not feel that his privileges had been breached. Beauchcsne continues as follows:
Even a gap of a few days may invalidate the claim for precedence in the House.
Therefore, on these grounds, which I am sure are quite obvious, I must rule that there is no question of privilege.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S OFFICE IN PARIS
speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware that the Paris, France, telephone directory in effect listed Quebec, prior to May 22, 1979, as an independent nation by referring to it as Ambassade du Quebec and, if so (a) what is the government doing to correct this falsehood with those concerned (b) is the government taking steps to determine whether or not Quebec's office in Paris has been granted certain diplomatic privileges such as duty-free liquor and cars, ordinarily granted only to recognized diplomatic personnel?
2.	Is the government aware that a press official of the French foreign ministry stated in a press interview in February of 1979 with reference to Quebec's house in Paris: "In effect, it's an embassy. Mr. Deschamps, the delegate general, is the equivalent of an ambassador" and, if so, what representations has or is the government making to the French government in this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S OFFICE IN PARIS
speechtext:
1. Yes. The government is aware that the Quebec office in Paris was so listed in the 1979 edition of Paris telephone directory, (a) The Canadian Embassy in Paris contacted the appropriate authorities on the subject. The Embassy learned that while this directory is published under the aegis of the French ministry of "Les Postes et Telecommunications", its content and marketing are in the hands of a private concern. The error was corrected in the 1980 edition of the Paris telephone directory, and the Quebec office in Paris no longer appears under the heading of "Ambassade". (b) The officers of the delegation enjoy privileges similar to those of international organizations. They were negotiated between the Canadian and French governments in the early sixties.
2.	Yes. The statement which was attributed to a press officer of the French foreign ministry was in fact made by the secretary of Quebec's Delegate-General in Paris. It expressed her own view of the situation rather than that of the Quebec government. No action is therefore required.

That this House welcomes the result of the referendum in Quebec and pledges itself to interpret that vote as a clear call for constitutional change.
He said: "Madame ie President," we decided to put on the order paper today a general motion which calls upon the House to recognize the vote in Quebec as a vote that called very clearly for constitutional change. We thought it was important to do that so that members of Parliament of all political parties had a chance to speak out in united voice about the kind of Canada they want to see in the future.
[ Translation]
On Tuesday May 20, it is clear, Madam Speaker, that the people of Quebec voted against the status quo. Like many other Canadians, they made known their wish to build a new country. It is important to realize that this is a second chance for the renewal of the Canadian federation.

I must compliment the Quebecois for their intelligent, peaceful and democratic debate. In many countries around the world, in many different societies, the problems we are dealing with here could result in war, killings, violence and unrest. In Canada our differences are a clash of ideas, not of guns; our differences are a clash of words, not of fists.
In this debate I do not want to speak of winners; I do not want to speak of losers. I want to speak about the future of my country, which I think is very promising.
I also want to compliment the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of our country who spoke in a very positive and magnanimous way the night of the referendum and here in the House yesterday. I want to compliment the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the leader of my party, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), for their openness and conciliatory attitude in the House of Commons and on referendum night in Quebec on May 20.
This is not a time for self-righteousness. It is not a time for English against the French. It is not a time for east against the west. It is not a time for the federal government against the provincial governments. It is not a time for farmer against worker. And it is not a time for one Canadian against another. But it is a time for all of us to work together, to seek a common consensus and a common compromise for the Canada of tomorrow. It is a time to build a country with a new federation that has a central government strong enough so that we can have economic equality among all the regions, yet a country that is flexible enough that all the regions have freedom to express their uniqueness and their differences.

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
In addition to constitutional change, we need an economic development plan that is fair to all provinces, and we need to patriate the Canadian economy so that we own and control the house we live in and we have a Canada owned by Canadians.

Finally, we need a change in attitude in Canada, one of understanding and co-operation among all the people of this country. We are a wealthy country, we have resources, we have the educated people, and with imagination, with constitutional and structural changes, we can build a country where we can feed, and provide adequate health care for, all our people; a country where we can help the poor and the underprivileged, where we can find a place for Indian, Inuit and our Metis people, where we can have a special place for Quebec and French Canadians, and where we can have a special place for and thrive on our multicultural background and make it all a part of a new Canada.
[ Translation]
It is important to understand that the result of the referendum is a clear indication of a will to change. As a majority of Yes votes would not have meant the end of the country, a majority of No votes is by no means a guarantee of survival, it is obvious that the 40 per cent of Quebeckers who voted Yes demand substantial change. We must keep in mind that the majority of those who voted No, that is nearly 60 per cent, also demand substantial constitutional change. Also, we must note that some of those who voted Yes are in favour of federalism, but said Yes for tactical and strategic reasons.

It is also very important, 1 believe, when one looks at the vote in Quebec, to recognize that the "Oui" vote was strongest among the young; the "Oui" vote was strongest among the educated, the leaders of tomorrow. This reinforces the urgency of change in our country, and the urgency of making changes as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
I believe that we do not have very long to find a solution, otherwise dissension across Canada may be impossible to stop.
Just think about what has happened in this country since 1967, Mr. Speaker. Let us take our minds back to the year 1967, our centennial year, a year of great promise and great hope, a year of celebration in our country.
[ Translation]
Since 1967, a year of festivities in the province of Quebec, it is clear that many citizens are not too happy with the status quo. Here are some examples from recent years. In 1968, the Parti Quebecois was formed. In 1976, it had become the government of Quebec, and four years later, the Parti Quebecois had managed to rally 40 per cent of the votes for a mandate to negotiate sovereignty-association. It is clear that
many Quebeckers are not happy with the status quo in Canada.

Since our celebration in 1967 we have seen in the west increasing unhappiness and the founding of several small separatist groups, political parties, including the Unionist party that hopes to make me and all of us in western Canada Americans, something that as a westerner I will fight against by arguing for legitimate change within a federation. I have nothing against my friends in the United States, but 1 want to remain a Canadian; I want to remain a Canadian now and a Canadian in the future.
A recent poll by the Canada West Foundation showed that 13 per cent of western Canadians wanted the west to separate from Canada and form a separate country, and I think that is very serious. Some 4 per cent wanted us to join the United States. A CBC poll conducted in Swift Current, in my province, showed that 19 per cent of the people there wanted a separate country and 6 per cent wanted to join the United States. I think that is evidence that western alienation and unhappiness is growing in our country.
Since our celebration in 1967 we have seen increasing unrest in Newfoundland to the point where a distinguished journalist named Charles Lynch recently described a speech by Premier Brian Peckford as sounding more separatist than Rene Levesque.
Since our celebration in 1967 the Indian, Inuit and native people of our country have been increasingly frustrated with their status in Canada. Last month the Indians asked to participate in constitutional talks and to have some of their rights enshrined in a new Canadian constitution. These and other frustrations in our country are very real, and they must be met. We do not meet them by constantly putting people down, by clubbing people on the head and by isolating them. That only fosters a feeling of anger, a feeling of discontent and a feeling of alienation in our country.

With respect to Quebec, neither my party nor 1 are in favour of sovereignty-association, and the leader of my party has said so many times in Parliament and across the country. But I must congratulate the present government of Quebec, as my leader did in Parliament last year, I believe, on other political decisions, such as the project to nationalize the asbestos company, the automobile insurance scheme, the labour legislation, the farming legislation and its position on the status of women and the highest minimum wage in North America as well as other progressive measures. All these things have been accomplished within the federal system. I also agree with the general principle of Bill 101.
Bill 101 guarantees as many, if not more, rights to the English in Quebec than many of the other provinces guarantee to the Francophones who live outside Quebec. The English
May 22, 1980

minority in Quebec has schools and school boards, while in provinces such as Ontario there are many French schools. But in spite of the fact that there are half a million Francophones in Ontario, they are not allowed to have their own school boards. Here in the national capital the parents of tens of thousands of young people who attend French schools are not allowed to have French language school boards.
Instead of condemning everything that is done by the Quebec government, as some have done by comparing that government to the governments of Cuba and Haiti, we should praise what is right, progressive and good and condemn and dissociate ourselves from that with which we disagree. As 1 say, we disagree very strongly with sovereignty-association.
1 was very happy to notice, in La Presse newspaper of May 17, just last Saturday, an article which quoted a former Liberal MNA who had been a cabinet minister in the province of Quebec. The gentleman was Victor Goldbloom who is an Anglophone from the Jewish minority group in Quebec.

And I quote the headline:
The PQ nationalism does not exclude minorities
The Quebec society is one which is very democratic.

When someone like Mr. Goldbloom makes a statement like that, we should take cognizance of the fact that, just because we disagree strongly with one of the concepts of a people, we do not have to condemn the whole direction of the people. [Translation]
Quebec is different. It is a distinct society by reason of its history, its language and its culture. Moreover, its school and judicial systems are different from those to be found elsewhere in Canada. In my view, a new constitution must recognize this difference.

There are many differences and many problems in western Canada as well. I have already referred to the growth of the separatist movement, the Unionist party and the like, all of which we oppose. However, our differences in the west are primarily of an economic nature. For a long time there has been an increasing economic alienation of western Canada from Ottawa and the government.
But western Canada is not monolithic in a cultural sense. One need only look to Alberta and Saskatchewan to see the many historical, cultural and institutional differences which exist in the prairies. In Saskatchewan there is a long history of co-operation, of public ownership and of public participation in the economy. In Alberta the orientation has gone in the other direction.
However, there are many problems which are similar. We have problems in agriculture. We fought to build a Canadian Wheat Board, and we want to keep a Crow rate as a statutory rate to help our farmers. We also want to process our food resources in the west, to build up an industrial base and process some of the raw materials of western Canada in
Constitutional Change
western Canada to provide our people with jobs and the resulting economic benefits. We would also like to have a freight rate system that is more fair and does not discriminate against western Canadians in the development of our goods.
In terms of the constitution, there are many things that the western Canadian premiers are now asking of Ottawa. Recently at a meeting in Lethbridge, Alberta, the four premiers issued a communique saying that resources should be under the control of the provinces, that the provinces should have more input and more control over communications in our land, and that the federal institutions should be reformed so that they reflect a more accurate make-up of our country which would allow for more provincial input into the institutions of Canada.
What the western premiers are saying is something that we will have to consider in the months and years ahead-that they want a certain devolution of power toward the provinces on the one hand and, on the other hand, a strengthening in the centre of provincial voices and provincial views so that the provinces could have some input into institutions such as the Supreme Court and the Bank of Canada. Perhaps the Senate could be changed to a council of the provinces, or something of that nature.
These are some of the feelings one finds in western Canada.
I stress very strongly that most of those feelings are directed toward forming a new country within a federation, a country which we all wish to keep together.
To all those, whether in Quebec, in western Canada, in the maritimes, who have lost faith in a federal arrangement for Canada and to all those who no longer believe that the Canadian federation can meet their needs, we of the New Democratic Party reply that a federal structure is the solution to the various problems that exist in this country. Having said that, Madam Speaker, we cannot accept either the constitutional status quo or a renewed status quo. On the contrary, we consider the new federation must reflect the values of democracy and social justice.
I would like to recall rapidly some of the advantages of a federal arrangement and point out at the same time why the NDP, our party and myself are convinced that this political formula is best for the future of Canada. It is particularly interesting to see that the first individuals who were politically inspired by the old principle "In union there is strength" were not the Fathers of Confederation but the Iroquois who created the first kind of federation in this country. They understood that a federal arrangement was a guarantee of greater stability. Today we can confirm that idea, a very, very important idea. A federation is a more solid alliance than a treaty of association between two or several sovereign states. Another advantage is the absence of monopoly over the political power. In a federation, the political power is divided among different

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
levels of governent and within a democratic framework; that constitutes the best defence against an authoritarian regime by nature and against an intensification of social conflicts. It was de Tocqueville who wrote, I think, and 1 quote:
I believe provincial institutions to be useful to ail peoples, but none seem to me to have a more real need of those institutions than those whose social system is democratic.
It seems obvious, Mr. Speaker, to the largest part of the people that a federal arrangement assures a certain economic viability that would not be present in other situations. I will give you only two proofs of that. The process of greater economic unity in Europe-and I am referring here to the European Economic Community-and second, the recognition by the leader of the Parti Quebecois himself, Rene Levesque, in his platform, of the necessity of an economic association between Quebec and Canada.
Finally, as another advantage, one must be aware that a federation is not necessarily incompatible with the development of the peoples that make it up. It is rather the structures of the federation and the ways in which governments use those structures that can create a form of oppression of minority groups. So, in theory, it is possible to conceive the existence of a development for political groups and peoples.
And, Mr. Speaker, even Mr. Rene Levesque, Premier of Quebec and leader of the Parti Quebecois, acknowledges that because a month ago he wrote in the April, '80 edition of the magazine iAction nationale, and I quote:
instead of the present regime, it may be possible, in theory, to imagine a form of renewed federalism. But this renewed federalism should aim at changing Quebec's place in a way that will not weaken it but strengthen it.
Rene Levesque said that a month ago.
In principle, we of the New Democratic Party are not against this proposition since we believe that the development of the people who make the Canadian federation should be promoted. And as far as the Quebec society is concerned, we believe that during the next negotiation round, the idea of a special place for Quebec in the renewed federation should not be ruled out.

Mr. Speaker, I want for a few more moments to digress from the sort of problem we often deal with in this House-the concrete world of taxes, inflation, unemployment, expenditures and so forth-and to address briefly a problem that is much less tangible but in my opinion all too real. This is the problem of attitude. It is very difficult to talk in concrete terms of attitude, but it is the problems of attitude and of perception that underlie the way in which the central government goes about using its power.
It seems to me that power concentrated in the centre has all too often taken on the shape and the image of the centre, rather than reflecting the reality of the regions. This is a multicultural country; our people have come from many lands. The people who settled and built my province, for example,
have names like Konkin, Fedorak, or Tchorzewski. Even when adopting the English language they have left their cultural mark. The differences between my province and Newfoundland and Ontario are not as marked as those that exist between Saskatchewan and Quebec, but they are there and they are important. Thus it is important that the central body, the institutions, reflect those differences. We have different cultural values in Canada and those differences should not be treated as an impediment to progress; they should be seen as an attribute in this country.
To return to the question of perception, we must at all times remember that what one culture defines as having great importance is not necessarily so defined by another culture; those things which one culture defines as having equal value are not necessarily so defined by other cultures. By not recognizing the existence of these differences, by not seeing them as attributes and by not incorporating them into policies and programs-those which we describe as universal as well as those we describe as regional-we run the risk of increasing the alienation and regional conflicts with which we are all too familiar.

speechtext:
I shall cite but two examples, Mr. Speaker. I hope they will not seem petty or frivolous as they are examples that are important to many people. I remember Robert Cliche. [Translation]
And I think that hon. members remember clearly Mr. Robert Cliche, who was once the leader of our party in the province of Quebec and a very well known judge-

He was very popular and an important figure in the province of Quebec. I remember when Robert Cliche talked about the housing program of CMHC. He mentioned that this agency of the central government was building houses in Quebec to architectural plans, which I suppose were adopted by officials in Ottawa, and which had incredibly small kitchens. Robert Cliche pointed out that in the homes of Quebeckers the kitchen has always been a very special place. It was and still is a focal point, a place of socializing, a place of conversation. All this was ignored by CMHC planners who designed houses with small kitchens. In the scheme of things, this is a small problem but 1 think it is indicative and symbolic of the much larger problem of attitude at the centre of the regions of this country.
Another example is the matter that was raised in the House three or four weeks ago by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky). This example is very important to the part of the country that 1 come from. I refer to the recent policy of the government of ending the Saturday morning postal service in rural communities. In a constituency like mine people really do not understand how the central government can be so ignorant of the importance of this service to the continued viability of their communities, and therefore to the continuation of a way of life that they value. In a small community of 200 or 300 people or even 3,000 people, Saturday is the day when people
May 22, 1980

come to town to shop, to visit, to socialize, to meet friends, neighbours and relatives, to go to the coffee shops and cafes, to go to the co-ops. They also go to the post office. All you have to do in a small community is stand in front of the post office on a Saturday morning and you will meet over half the residents. That is important to us, Mr. Speaker. A lot of people feel alienated when such a service is removed.
Whether we talk about housing programs, the postal service, rail policy or a multitude of other policies and programs, the widespread feeling that the central government is literally and figuratively too far removed from the lives and aspirations of the diverse people of this country is, it seems to me, justified. Too much has been undertaken by planners and mandated by governments which indicates that there is no awareness or appreciation of the differing values in this country.
As we set out on this ground project of constitutional reform, we must begin, as the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, by putting our own house in order and by putting our own institutions in order. We can begin that process by making sure that our perception of what this country is all about is correct. I think that all of us in this Elouse realize how easy it is to lose sight of what is wanted in the constituencies when we are burdened with the administrative and other responsibilities of office. We must take steps to ensure that the voices of all the peoples and all the regions are heard and that their aspirations are realized as much as possible.
I see that my time is about up, Mr. Speaker. If you will allow me another minute or two, I should like to conclude by saying that the task before us is no easy one. I think we have started off with the right tone, however. We started off by being open, by wanting to build bridges, wanting to reach out to people, wanting to build a federation with a centre strong enough to make sure we have genuine equality of opportunity, yet flexible enough that each region and each province can demonstrate its uniqueness. That uniqueness can grow and flower, Mr. Speaker, and make all of us better and more wealthy because of it.
We are a string of communities, a string of regions and a string of cultures around this country. The combination of all those cultures and communities is more than just the literal addition of them. We are more than a community of communities. The combination of all of that is Canada. It is the combination of all of that that 1 think is going to make this country one of the really great countries in the years that lie ahead.
I plead with the Prime Minister, with members of this House, with all of the provincial premiers and leaders, that in the next few weeks and in the next couple of years-because I believe that we do not have too many more years to go-we maintain this policy of openness, this policy of trying to draft a new constitution, a new framework with new economic policies, with new attitudes that will make us, once again, one big, united family that recognizes our differences, that is proud of those differences and that grows because of those differences.
Constitutional Change
Those are differences that make us a country called Canada that is unique and prosperous in the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to congratulate the hon. member who moved the motion now before the House as the topic to be discussed on this allotted day. It is very simple and, if I may, I should like to read it again:
That this House welcomes the result of the referendum in Quebec-
Obviously, as far as the first part of the motion is concerned, as we saw yesterday, the reaction was spontaneous and unanimous on both sides of the House: all hon. members from all parts of Canada, are truly happy with that result. 1 resume the quotation:
-and pledges itself to interpret that vote as a clear call for constitutional change.
The second statement is also obvious in that the reaction of the hon. members of all parties proved clearly yesterday in this House that the results of the vote in the province of Quebec must be interpreted as proof that the province of Quebec has decided to choose Canada while at the same time calling for a renewed federalism.
As far as I am concerned, the way I interpret the results which gave the federalist forces about 60 per cent of the votes in Quebec as opposed to 40 per cent to the Yes forces, is this, Mr. Speaker: they are clearly indicative of two conclusions. The first, that a large majority of Quebeckers have expressed their wish to remain within Canada; and second, that a large majority of Quebeckers have also heard, accepted and understood our message to the effect that by voting No, they would be voting for major constitutional change. If, in addition, we take into account the fact that amongst those who voted Yes, quite a number did so, by their own admission, to exert pressure with a view to getting a renewed federalism and those people wanted change while remaining within Canada, in the final analysis, we see that, in that May 20 referendum, far more than 60 per cent of the Quebeckers indicated clearly that they choose to belong to Canada. Therefore, my interpretation is that the vast majority of Quebeckers chose Canada Tuesday night, but that they did so in the hope that institutions can now be changed in the near future. And what leads me to come to that conclusion is the style that permeated the referendum campaign in Quebec these last few weeks. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the campaign unofficially began by the tabling of the notorious question in the Legislature, to be followed subsequently by a debate. All the observers that I have met, at least a large number of them, agree that during the debate in the Quebec legislature the PQ members did not deal at length in their speeches with the question itself but mostly discussed matters other than sovereignty-association. Conversely, the opposition members, a much smaller group,

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
denounced the question as being ambiguous, long, confusing and designed to garner votes under misrepresentations. But since the PQ members were in a majority situation in the legislature, it so happened that their comments had an impact on the public and indeed at that stage of the referendum campaign, the PQ had taken the lead and was winning over the federalist forces.
After that, the referendum campaign was officially launched and then a strange phenomenon happened. Many would have thought that it would have been hard for federalist forces to rally, but quite the opposite. In fact, federalist forces came together and united in the most perfect harmony and in the strongest unity to take a united stand against the sovereignty approach. Under Mr. Ryan's remarkable leadership, we saw the Liberal members of the Quebec National Assembly, the members of the National Union and of other opposition parties join forces with members of this Parliament and in the most complete harmony express to all Quebeckers their will to build a modern Canada, a country that meets the requirements of its regions and where the constitution will be renewed as soon as possible.
This was a turning point because, from the very beginning of the referendum campaign, we saw the exemplary union of federalist forces of all parties both in Quebec and in Canada and this, to my mind, largely contributed to the great victory of the No vote during the referendum campaign.
Also, the style adopted by both forces was a determining factor in the decision made by the voters in the province of Quebec. If we analyse briefly the campaign style of the Parti Quebecois and the Yes side, we realize, and this may seem paradoxical, that their approach was very negative. I suggest that this seems paradoxical because they were trying to get a Yes answer, while their approach was essentially negative.
The Yes supporters attacked federalism, federalists, and they even tried in some instances to attack individuals rather than to stick to the substance of the debate. They even failed- and it was perhaps a strategy, and if so, it failed-to deal in depth with sovereignty-association and to define it to a population which was obviously concerned and wanted to know exactly where the Parti Quebecois and the Yes supporters wanted to lead them with a question which was denounced from the very beginning of the campaign as deceptive and ambiguous.
And we saw on May 20 how the general public's common sense had the better end. The question itself aroused suspicion, being much too long and not really understandable by the average Quebec men and women, the average citizens. And the people told themselves: If the question is so long and complex, probably those who put it have something in the back of their minds. I think this was a natural reaction by Quebeckers, at least in my constituency.
It would have been much simpler to ask plainly: Do you support sovereignty-association or not? and explain the
implications during the campaign. The skepticism caused by the lengthy and ambiguous question was strengthened by the fact that the question was being put by a political party proposing Quebec's independence. Federalist forces made this very clear in my view during the referendum campaign when bringing it to the attention of Quebeckers. Finally the people from the Parti Quebecois used their majority position to force their question upon the National Assembly and in the referendum.
And Quebeckers realized that the lengthy and difficult question, ambiguous for most people, was put by a political party with a clear platform to seek independence for Quebec. Once again the common sense of the people prevented them from going the Parti Quebecois' way, not only because the question was confusing and too lengthy, but also because it was put by a party with an avowed objective of independence that appeared to be hiding their choice behind a 125-word question.
But something more decisive than the ambiguity and length of the question and the fact it was put by a political party seeking independence is that Yes forces, the PQ majority failed to show Quebeckers-as theirs was the burden of proof that the change to sovereignty-association would bring about advantages not provided by the current system, federalism, and I think that the No forces exploited that well in all regions, and the question was legitimate. 1 think that with a question as important as this one where people were asked to give the government the mandate to negotiate sovereignty-association, a question which was 125 words long, and that was what the Parti Quebecois wanted, 1 think it would have been normal and wise for the Yes side, during the referendum campaign, to try and prove to the ordinary people, to the general public that a change was desirable because it would benefit Quebeckers.
Not only was proof not given by but the Yes forces, those who argued for the Yes cause, seem to have deliberately avoided talking about sovereignty-association and therefore about its advantages, if any. This, in my opinion, showed disrespect for the electorate and the people of Quebec. But once again, as 1 have said, common sense prevailed. Quebeckers were distrustful as soon as the question was made public because it was long, because it was ambiguous, because it was asked by a political party whose political option was to achieve independence, and it seems to me that the fact that the Pequistes skirted the definition of sovereignty-association and its consequences only added to this mistrust and encouraged the great majority of Quebeckers to reject the option, to refuse to give the mandate asked for and to say no to the referendum question. So, this is my modest and very summary analysis of the results of the referendum, results that should be interpreted as an outright rejection of sovereignty-association by Quebeckers, an option unknown to them and about which they have been systematically denied any explanation and, conse-
May 22, 1980

quently, of which they do not know the benefits, if any. On the other hand the results of the vote show very clearly and very positively that the huge majority of Quebeckers are in favour of Canada, their feeling of belonging was very obvious but, at the same time, most Quebeckers, if you add up to those who voted No all those who voted Yes and who wanted constitutional changes but within the federation, we realize that the large majority of Quebec citizens want major constitutional changes and very soon.
I am delighted with the result because it makes two things clear; first, that a majority of Quebeckers have expressed their preference for staying in Canada; and second, that they have heard and accepted our message that voting No is a vote for change. In interpreting this victory we should remember that many people who voted Yes really want change which would keep Quebec in Canada. So, all in all, the victory for Canada is clear. The job now is to get on with the work of reform as rapidly as we can, and this is exactly what we intend to do. It is our hope that the government of Quebec will accept the will of the people and express its willingness to participate creatively in the work of constitutional reform.

It made me conclude that the large majority of Quebeckers want to stay in Canada and promote a renewed federalism. 1 mentioned the type of campaign made by the Yes supporters, but the type of campaign of the No supporters had also an influence and a significant one.
On our side, I think we tried to make people proud of belonging to Canada and we have been very successful. 1 think people in Quebec accepted our proposal that they should choose the road that the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada, (Mr. Trudeau) had often described as the road to excellence, where you try to be heard at the federal level so that this country will be governed in harmony between the two great founding peoples and so that individual freedoms and minority rights will be protected.
I think that our commitment to Canada and our approach commanded great respect, because people understood what we were asking from them, in spite of injustices that occurred in the past which no one denies, but that nonetheless happened within a relatively very short period of time. After all, in my humble point of view, a nation is still very young when it is only 113 years old. There are various ways of correcting injustices. Contrary to the Parti Quebecois, which was advocating a kind of territorial withdrawal which would be an act of frustration and would result in the loss for the Quebec people of huge resources, both cultural and material, and which would also be unfair to our French-speaking minorities outside of Quebec, what we were proposing was-instead of collective sulking and a sort of confinement in a limited territory-a noble effort to show that in this country which is still very young, French and English people can live in com-
Constitutional Change
plete harmony, in mutual respect, and of course in the greatest equality, Mr. Speaker. 1 for one believe in it, and think that our message was well accepted by the Quebec people as a whole. In 1980, in a country which is about 113 years old, we can still meet the challenge of diversity or, in other words, as 1 have just said, allow two great founding people to benefit from the cultural wealth of each other and let several other cultures be respected and develop in the Canadian mosaic. I believe that what 1 said in my region, and what many others said in their own region, helped to strengthen the will of Quebeckers to meet this challenge, to have confidence in the future and to go on building a great country which can remain united and be really strong. I have the impression that the vote on the question asked by the Parti Quebecois resulted in a refusal of the concept of sovereignty-association, but also, and this can now be stated as an obvious fact, gave massive support to a healthy, fair and equitable development of the beautiful and vast country which is Canada. This this is why I am in complete agreement with my colleague of the New Democratic Party who moved today's motion when he concluded, as 1 am convinced we must all conclude, that it is now obvious that Canadian attitudes have begun to change clearly and significantly, and I believe that this will lead to constitutional changes which will come about effectively and quickly. I am happy that the Prime Minister unequivocally reaffirmed yesterday in this House his desire to bring about a renewed constitution and the flexibility of his approach.
Before closing, 1 would not want to miss the opportunity to quote some of his comments which are essential at this stage of the evolution of our Canadian history. Two days ago, we saw the victory of the No option of which we have just commented on the meaning for Quebec, but the fight is not over. It has just begun, Mr. Speaker. It is important to emphasize this short passage of the statement made yesterday afternoon in the House by the Prime Minister of Canada, and I quote:
-I have asked the Minister of Justice to begin immediately a tour of the provincial capitals in order to obtain the views of the premiers on the best way to follow up on their will to change. As for us, our only prerequisites for change are the two which I outlined in Quebec as early as January, 1977.
First, that Canada continue to be a real federation, a state whose constitution establishes a federal Parliament with real powers applying to the country as a whole and provincial legislatures with powers just as real applying to the territory of each province. Second, that a charter of fundamental rights and freedoms be entrenched in the new constitution and that it extend to the collective aspect of these rights, such as language rights.
1 had said at the time and 1 say again today that we consider everything else to be negotiable. What we want is to give Canada a new, modern and functional federal constitution which will enable our governments to better meet the needs and aspirations of all Canadians.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is hardly anything left to add to the comments made by the Prime Minister of Canada; except for the federal link as well as individual and minority rights, everything else is negotiable. This is where we stand and I have every reason to believe that with some good will, a change of attitude has been shown and continues to be shown, but now it is time to alter our institutions in a harmonious climate without undue delay.

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
