subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate. I want to say at the outset that the official opposition fully endorses the two elements of the motion before the House this afternoon.
The citizens of Quebec have spoken clearly and expressed their desire to remain in Canada. For many the referendum was an experience in which they shared very deeply. But the outpouring of emotion was not restricted to the citizens of Quebec. Across Canada Canadians have expressed relief and gratitude at the results, which were a clear demonstration that the break-up of Canada was not to proceed, that sovereignty-association was not an option that we would consider.
Now that the referendum is over, it is imperative that Canadians from all parts of the country have an opportunity to
May 22, 1980

participate in the changes that must take place. As Canadians, first, we must recognize that we are among the most fortunate countries of the world. Yes, we have problems; yes, changes must be made in our institutions; but let us never forget that as a nation we have advantages. We have been blessed beyond the dreams of those who in the 1860s gave form to our country.
Second, we must remember that confederation has not failed. During the past 113 years our country has developed into a modern society, a society which is conscious of its minorities, a society which gives everyone opportunities unequalled anywhere else in the world today.
There have been those who have argued that confederation does not and has not worked, those who have advocated that a province or a region would have a better future if it were on its own. Canadian history is replete with examples of politicians who have advocated the dismemberment of our country. Those politicians of division are still with us today, but they have never been able to convince the majority of Canadians, who have followed their own common sense, to follow their siren call for ending the Canadian experience. Often they were motivated by frustration or perceived injustice which they felt was perpetrated on their region or on their province. But never were Canadians willing to follow their proposition that our future would be better apart and that we should end the grand experiment called Canada.
The Fathers of Confederation grappled with attitudes and problems similar to those that face us today. Tension then, as today, existed between English and French-speaking Canadians, and even then between east and west. But I am reminded of the words of one of the Fathers of Confederation, George Etienne Cartier, when he said in 1865:
Shall we be content to maintain a mere provincial existence, when by combining together we could become a great nation?
Surely that is the sentiment of every member of the Elouse and also virtually every Canadian, that we are a great nation only because we have combined together in a common cause.
Just as in 1867 Canadian leaders saw the need and the advantage of joining together and forming a new nation, so also today that advantage has not changed. It is important, therefore, that we renew our dedication to the building of our country. Having said that, let me say that it is important that we grasp this moment of opportunity. The important question must be answered not by words but by action.
Many supporters of the No option were convinced to vote No because of the promise of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other federal leaders that constitutional change would become a priority. Additionally, a significant number of those who voted Yes were convinced that the only way in which constitutional change could take place was by voting Yes and delivering a shock to Ottawa to get on with the job.
Constitutional change should not be viewed by either the federal government or the provinces as an exercise where one has to give up or give in, but rather as an exercise in nation building. It does not have to be a win-lose confrontation. What
Constitutional Change
is fundamental is the attitude that will be brought to the exercise.
In the past many of us have said that the Prime Minister has been inflexible in his approach to constitutional change. The attitude to adopt must be one which embraces openness and the willingness to see the other person's point of view. It is an attitude which cannot be dominated by a win-at-any-cost approach. Unfortunately, our history is littered with the debris of constitutional proposals and conferences which attempted to bring about constitutional renewal but were not successful because of the attitude of the participants. In the end, if people are not willing to change their attitudes, no matter which structures we anticipate, no matter what conferences we call, they will end in failure.
Speaking in the House yesterday, my leader said, in terms of attitude:
More than the law and more than the constitution is at issue here. There must also be a positive attitude among citizens and among governments, an attitude which is consistent with the changes in law and the changes in form.
First of all, then, we must accept that the status quo as now understood is not acceptable. A genuine feeling exists that a new constitution is needed for Canada, a constitution in Canada which can be amended by Canadians.
It is for these reasons that it is important to reach out to those Quebeckers who voted and who wanted to see constitutional renewal. It is important that we do not reject those who, because of their frustration, voted Yes but who did not want to end the federalist experience.
Despite the euphoria and good will that have poured out throughout Canada and in this House since May 20, 1 believe that a word of caution must be expressed. Of course we want constitutional renewal, and the referendum vote should be interpreted exactly that way. But there is an inherent danger that we can create false expectations that constitutional renewal will be easy to achieve and that, once achieved, the structural problems will not give rise to new frustrations. We must also be cautious that we do not give the impression that constitutional change will end the differences and the divisions which have occurred in the past.
Second, it is important to stress that this desire for change is not only a Quebec phenomenon. My leader said in the House recently:
May 20 was but a date in a continuing process. It is by no means an end but a beginning, and now it is up to us in this Parliament and in the parliament of the territories and the provinces of Canada to implement changes which are being sought by Canadians all across this country.
We cannot make the mistake that only Quebec wants change. Nor can we fall into the trap that one region has more legitimate grievances than another. Just because certain regions have not chosen to have similar referendums does not indicate less determination to address and alleviate long-standing grievances.
So at this time of good will we also face a serious peril-a real threat that disappointment and anger can replace this goodwill if we fritter away our opportunities. All of us recognize how quickly good will can be replaced by anger and

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
accusations. We must avoid giving any comfort to the separatists, wherever they may be, to conduct our activities in such a way that the talks would not lead to new satisfactory arrangements. There are obviously people in this country who are hoping that these talks will end in failure. This cannot happen. The talks must be real and they must bear results.
Additionally, we must caution members of the House that results will not be achieved overnight. We can pass as many unanimous resolutions in the House as we want; these will not result in overnight change, it will also take more than a few months. While there may be advantages to setting target dates, I for one would caution members of the House that the setting of strict time limits by which renewals should occur has inherent dangers in it. There have been premiers, as well as members of this House, who have said that within two years a new constitutional renewal could take place. While targets are acceptable, 1 do not think we should be locked into those kinds of time frames.
Yesterday the Prime Minister, when speaking in this House, stated that a federal-provincial conference would be called in the near future for the purpose of discussing the future of Canada. While we welcomed this announcement, it is important that we note the manner in which these conferences have functioned in the past. They have provided a forum for leaders from all regions of Canada to meet and discuss the problems the country faces. This exchange of views has been beneficial.
But there is also an inherent weakness in this approach. For one, these conferences provide a forum in which to express grievances as well as to put forward points of view, but unfortunately too often they have not brought about resolution of conflicts. Some might say that this is a harsh judgment of the federal-provincial history of this country, but a study of that history will show many of these conferences failed. While the participants were well-meaning, the legacy of the conferences did not result in the changes sought by the people. By their very nature the membership is composed of political leaders who must defend provincial or federal interests. Too often those interests have thwarted any compromise that could have broken the impasse.
Additionally, these conferences are composed of personalities, and often the personalities have been in conflict with other participants around the table. A reality of a democratic society is also that these participants from time to time face elections. They have to meet the people. That as well can result in positions taken which, through other circumstances, might not have been pressed as hard.
Yesterday in this House questions were asked of the government as to whether consideration was being given to expanding the format of constitutional conferences after the initial federal-provincial conference to be held later this year. My view is that consideration should be given to expanding the membership in these meetings into a broader-based constitutional meeting which would include political leaders other than the Prime Minister and the premiers. The hon. Leader of the
Opposition (Mr. Clark), the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), and for that matter elected leaders in the provinces, represent a large number of Canadians as well as regions which this government does not represent in this House.
I welcome the assurances of the Prime Minister to consult with the Leader of the Opposition with a view to exploring the possibility of expanding the format. As well, consideration should be given to including representation of groups in Canada that have a special interest in constitutional change. I think all of us know there are many of them and they seem to be increasing every day.
The suggestion of Premier Hatfield on the night of the referendum that a regular schedule of meetings be considered is a worth-while proposal. I think it would be advantageous to have regularly scheduled meetings rather than a target date by which constitutional renewal must take place.
One must ask the question: What do Canadians want in a new constitution? I believe many of the grievances we have heard in the past are not constitutional in nature but rather are due to frustration from governmental agencies, regulatory bodies and government in general not serving the interests of Canadians. For example, membership on many of these agencies does not reflect the regions and does not reflect the participation that the various members of those regions would like to give. If the federal government is interested in retaining the status quo, the bureaucracy with all its resources will reflect that attitude and will further frustrate Canadians.
There has been a difference of opinion between my leader and the present Prime Minister on the role the regions should play. Let it be clearly understood that my leader and this party have never stood for the dismantling of the federal government. Rather, we want to see it strengthened. We want a strong federal government that can address and resolve national issues; let there be no doubt about that. The reference of the Prime Minister of "Who speaks for Canada?" in my mind was a divisive attempt meant to reflect on my leader-that he was not interested in preserving national institutions. Nothing could be further from the truth. Rather it was a recognition by my leader and our party that strong regions contribute to a stronger country. Strong regions are not a threat to Canada. A strong Atlantic Canada with strong economic bases is of advantage to all of us. A strong western Canada, building on its resources and its agricultural base, is of benefit to all and should be recognized as such.
During this debate other members of my party will address the issue of constitutional renewal from the perspective of their constituents and their regions. I want to spend some time dealing with the views we hear expressed in western Canada.
Much has been said of the deep-seated resentment in western Canada. Let there be no doubt that the resentment toward the manner in which the federal government has ignored western Canada runs very deeply. It is not an accident that the government does not enjoy representation west of Winnipeg. How many members of Parliament from western Canada have stood in this House, from one Parliament to the next, and read
May 22, 1980

the history or litany of grievances which we experience in western Canada? I do not have to repeat them; everybody knows them. But it is important that we recognize that those grievances are legitimate. They are as legitimate as the aspirations of the people of any other region of Canada.
For example, only recently there were promises made during the election campaign, promises that were changed, promises that were called into doubt or promises that were cancelled. It is that attitude which has resulted in the alienation we now feel.
But underlying specifics such as provincial control over resources, lack of secondary industry, or the loss of comparative or competitive advantage in the western freight rates, there is a deeper feeling of grievance. It is, that expressions of our aspirations, the grievances we have had in the past, have been interpreted in this House and in federal institutions as not being as valid as the grievances of other areas. I stand in this House not simply as a representative of western Canada. 1 stand here as a representative in the federal House of Canada. Let there be no mistake about it: we cannot nor will we accept that the points we want to make and the building to which we want to contribute should in any way be lessened because we come from western Canada, or that our grievances are not valid today because they have been repeated so often. It is important to remember that the west wants to grow, but it does not want to grow at the expense of Ontario or any other part of Canada. Rather we see our growth as benefiting the entire country. Western Canadians share the View that federalism is based upon the concept of sharing. We want to do our part and we will do our part. 1 ask this government to change its ways, not to hold us back or be less interested in us than other regions.
1 want to spend some time in consideration of Canadians whose background is neither French nor English. It must be clearly understood that Canadians who are recent immigrants, or who have been here for a few generations first and foremost want to be Canadians. The referendum period for them, even though they did not live in Quebec, was traumatic because many of them had come to Canada to escape deep-seated and long-standing animosities in their homelands. They came here because they wanted stability. Too often they had been forced to leave because basic human rights in their homelands had been violated, or radical changes either in government or in their boundaries had taken place. These people look upon constitutional renewal as a strengthening of our federal system to create stability and the preservation of human rights.
The Prime Minister has stated his determination to enshrine a bill of rights in the constitution. He mentioned that in the House yesterday as well. It is my view that no greater contribution could be made by the Prime Minister to those Canadians of whom 1 have just spoken than incorporating the bill of rights of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker into the new constitution.

Constitutional Change

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
During the time when I had responsibilities as minister of Indian affairs and northern development I became acutely aware of another region of Canada that is too often left out of the mainstream of Canadian life, and I speak of the two Canadian territories. The north also wants to be part of this renewal in Canada. The north is an awakening giant, an area which gives us an opportunity to be nation builders. When one takes a look at the various countries of the world one sees that Canada is one of the few that has a frontier where we can still build as a nation.
Residents of the north, be they native or white, want to be Canadians first. They do not want to be colonists of the federal government. The time has long passed when commissioners can be appointed to make decisions without regard to the residents or their representatives. The north will develop institutions that are similar to ours, but they will be modified to reflect the native population and the special conditions that exist north of 60.
Another contribution this House could make, and we as members of it, is that we not stand in the way of native people and residents of the north by deciding for them what is best from the view of those of us in the south.
I face the future of Canada with great optimism. A country is more than a constitution and it is more than its institutions; it is a feeling, it is one of belonging and it is personal.
Speaking personally, if I could for just a minute, I had been in Quebec City a number of times prior to when the right hon. former prime minister asked me to serve in his cabinet. We had a cabinet meeting in Quebec City. That was the first time it was impressed upon me that I, as the son of an immigrant, was able to be in that part of Canada and look at the shores of the St. Lawrence River where my father had landed 50 years before without any future other than the hope this country gave him, and to realize 50 years later that this country had given me an opportunity to serve.
There are opportunities that this country gives each of us in a unique way. I am filled with hope that we will grasp the opportunity that awaits us. This is a growing country, a young country and a country that is facing change; but our future must be one of a united nation, from sea to sea and from our border to the Arctic.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 too welcomed the decision of the people of Quebec to vote No in the referendum on Tuesday. This was a result which indicated a love for Canada and a faith in this nation on the part of the residents of that region. The good will felt by the rest of Canada toward Quebec as a consequence of this decision provides an opportunity to make real progress in the next round of constitutional talks.
This opportunity is also a challenge, because if we do not make significant headway now the negative feelings the previous speaker mentioned, which are real, and the feeling of hopelessness on constitutional talks, will be felt not only by the Quebecois but by all Canadians. There is presently a hope in our ability to overcome the obstacles which have created

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
roadblocks in the past and that we now must meet in order to face the challenge we have as a nation.
We face more than one challenge, and we must be clear about that. Constitutional talks do not deal with just the Quebec issue, although naturally recent events have tended to focus on that particular problem which we face as a country. There are other issues: Native people were not involved in the formulation of the original BNA Act or amendments that have since come into place. They now wish to have full participation in discussions which will affect their future as well. We cannot straitjacket ourselves or our country by believing that we will solve all the problems of all the people of Canada by discussions among 11 men. Constitutional change in Canada must include participation by native Canadians. They are too often left out of any constitutional discussions and considerations by government.
Fortunately, recent federal governments, both Liberal and Conservative, have realized that the aspirations of native people within Canada must be taken seriously. Unfortunately, recent governments have not come to any conclusion about the exact nature of the role of native people at the discussion tables.
It was just a little over ten years ago that the then Liberal federal government concluded that the best way to deal with native problems and native aspirations was by a mainstreaming approach, by an assimilating approach. If I may refer to a Liberal policy paper at that time, the so-called "Chretien white paper" of 1969, it said that all these conditions of the Indians are the product of history and have nothing to do with their abilities and capabilities. Indian relations with other Canadians began with special treatment by government and society, and special treatment has been the rule since Europeans first settled in Canada. Special treatment has made the Indians a community disadvantaged and apart. Obviously the course of history must be changed. Just ten years ago that was the policy of the Canadian government.
In the short run what they were saying was that the Indian Act, enacted under the authority of section 91 of the British North America Act, should be repealed, and in the long run that the policy of the federal government implied that ultimately any specific references to Indians must be removed. That approach would have meant that the native people would have no role in constitutional talks had they taken place ten years ago. Today, ten years later, the federal government does realize that exclusion will not mean positive change for native people. What it has not figured out is just how native people will be consulted in the constitutional talks.
In his speech last month to the national conference of Indian chiefs and elders, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised that his government would be working closely with Indian representatives in any reform of the Canadian constitution. The fact is that the Prime Minister's remarks could have as easily referred to any single Canadian or any other group within our society. It is not our business to rank the various
social and ethnic groups in order of their capacity or their status at the negotiating table, but at the very least we will have to recognize that Canada's native people are Canada's original residents and are, therefore, entitled to full participation in any constitutional talks.
The Prime Minister's remarks last month have, quite frankly, proven unacceptable to the native people of this country. The New Democratic Party recognizes that this country's obligations to some of its native people are written in the treaties, but that those treaty rights are not there for the Inuit or the Metis people of this country. Aboriginal rights, such as those pertaining to hunting, fishing and land use, are well documented but they are not accepted by many Canadians. The current land claims negotiations have a grounding in historic precedent and in law but are not showing any progress.
Therefore, it is certain that the fairest and most just way of recognizing Indian input is not by excluding them from participating or by hoping that the problems will melt away, as suggested in the white paper. Instead, native participation must be full and ongoing in future negotiations.
We are all partners in confederation, and if our obligations to Canada's original people are not made clear in constitutional talks, then confederation will be a misnomer for native people. I would hope that in his trip across the nation to meet with the provincial leaders, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) will also meet with representatives of the native people of Canada.
Northern residents are also concerned about the future of this country. Northern residents in this vast country have expectations about their role in constitutional change. Residents of the territories, both white and native, cannot be excluded from determinations that affect their future. To do that would be a denial of the principle of self-determination, that somehow others will express the concerns of northerners without being elected representatives of the people living in those regions. Northern residents in the territories, as in the northern regions of most provinces, have concerns that must be addressed in any constitutional changes. Decisions regarding how economic development will take place should not be left to those living elsewhere in Canada or, worse, to those living outside our borders.
In addition, just as the railway to the Pacific was a condition before British Columbia would enter confederation, we must provide certain initiatives, such as equalized freight rates and guaranteed medical services, to enable northerners to be part of the economic growth of our country and to benefit from those social services which we believe all Canadians are entitled to as a basic minimum standard. Such social services are sadly lacking in many northern communities and are a disgrace in light of our relative affluence as a nation. This is a serious problem. There are other serious problems which can be resolved or at least partly resolved as a result of constitutional talks.
Another problem which we face is in the area of regional disparity. Regional disparity is a serious challenge to the unity of this country. If we are able to continue living together in a
May 22, 1980

confederation and if we are to consider ourselves a united composite of different regions, we will have to recognize that serious regional disparities are there and that we must do something about them. These disparities are nothing less than a product of a century of patchwork economic development in this country. They are representative of a lack of a national policy and planning that is based on our resources.
The examples of regional disparity are many. The northern part of this country has been the site of resource extraction with little planning and with little benefit to the residents of those regions. If we are to live together in this community of Canada, we must begin to place development in the north in its proper perspective. It must be development not just for the sake of development. It must be development not just for the sake of the south and central parts of Canada, but development which is also for the sake of the north. Inevitably this will mean that some development will not take place because it would be detrimental to the north and its inhabitants. Sometimes we will find that certain developments should take place that will be of social and economic benefit to the northern regions, but that they will need the assistance of the provinces, the territories and the federal government in order to bring about that development.
In other parts of the country there are also regional disparities. The Atlantic provinces have traditionally been an area where regional disparity has hurt the unity of this nation. A specific example there can be found in the industrial Cape Breton area where the Sydney Steel Corporation plant is not operating at the capacity of which it is capable. The province of Nova Scotia alone cannot provide the input to ensure that jobs are protected and that the Sysco plant is modernized. This requires federal government assistance. So far the federal government has been reluctant to keep its part of the bargain. In order to prevent an economic downturn in Cape Breton which would isolate it from the well-being of Canada, the provincial and federal governments must work together.
Any changes in the framework of our constitution must allow for provincial and federal projects to overcome present regional disparity. Changes in our constitution cannot be allowed if they result in the federal government being too weak or too impoverished to assist in the development of the entire nation. After all, the federal-provincial conferences of the past have not really produced the results for which we have asked. It has been a long process which has been very difficult and frustrating for many Canadians.
I would question whether or not we really knew what we wanted in our constitution over this past decade. Are we simply to move some items from section 91 to section 92 and back again? Are we simply to make cosmetic changes that will create an illusion of progress? Or are we to have a constitution that will soothe the various wounds that open from time to time in this country, or is the constitution to be a foundation for creating the type of Canada that we want for ourselves and for future generations?
Of course, we hope that we will accept the latter choice, for if we do we will not only avoid the pitfalls of continuous
Constitutional Change
tinkering with a delicate instrument like the constitution, but we will also be able to use our energies to build a nation in which we will all be able to exercise our cultural and economic goals. In this respect I would like to remind hon. members that historically what has been called English Canada has always been a generation behind French Canadians in determining its own aspirations.
At the beginning of this century Henri Bourassa, as an MP in this House, rose to call for a Canadian identity. He was rebuked by those who wished to remain part of the British Empire. Twenty years later we accepted the wisdom of Bou-rassa's remarks. When Quebec premiers called out for the strengthening of the role of the provinces within confederation, the rest of the country ignored them and was appalled at the thought. A generation later we heard the same call coming from each and every region of this country. In the sixties when Quebec was asking to be maitre chez nous or master of their own destiny, the rest of Canada was accepting increased foreign control of our resources, our industry and our future. It has ofter been said that Quebec wants too much independence and that English Canada wants none. We are now in the 1980s and another generation has passed by. It is time for all Canadians to be asking to be masters of their own destiny.
How we resolve the Quebec issue and the other problems that we face, not only the answers that we arrive at but the process which we go through, can be an example to others in this world. The referendum held on Tuesday with its unique approach and its peaceful progress was historic in a world where such decisions are usually made through use of the bayonet. Where we go from here will be of importance in history.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank my party leader for suggesting that we use our opposition day-which is normally an opportunity to score political points-in a nonpartisan manner to give members of the House an opportunity to discuss this important issue.
In a similar way I hope that the Prime Minister and the premiers will realize that 11 people cannot answer all the questions that the nation must ask of itself. With that in mind I would encourage the first ministers to take the approach suggested by the leader of my party yesterday and form delegations that are non-partisan in approach and membership to discuss future constitutional action. The need for this was made very obvious in the House this afternoon. The first three speakers from the opposition all represented western ridings while the government speakers represented eastern ridings. That is a result of the composition of this House.
The mood of the country is open to changes in the constitution, especially after the decision of Tuesday night. This openness to change, however, might well dissipate if all points of view are not aired in an open and non-partisan manner. The only way to decide our future, Mr. Speaker, is to work at it together.

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin this speech, which is the first opportunity 1 have had to address this House at length, by extending my warmest congratulations to Madam Speaker on her election to the very important office she now holds.
As a new member of Parliament I am honoured to be a participant in a debate on constitutional reform.
I believe it is customary, Mr. Speaker, for a newly elected member to share with the House a few observations about the nature of the riding he or she represents. In describing Kitchener, 1 cannot help but feel a very deep sense of pride in the history and accomplishments of the city I grew up in. 1 also feel a strong sense of responsibility, as the voters of Kitchener have placed a trust in me to voice their concerns and make a contribution on their behalf to this Parliament.
Kitchener in many ways is a microcosm of Canada-a cultural kaleidoscope of the Canadian experience. Many people associate my riding with Canadians of German descent. They comprise 32 per cent of our city's population. Oktober-fest, for which our city is now famous, rivals its predecessor in Munich. People of Irish, English and Scottish extraction comprise 45 per cent of my constituents. Twenty three per cent of Kitchener's residents are largely those whose ancestry is French, Polish, Dutch, Italian, Portuguese, Ukrainian, Chinese, Japanese, East and West Indian, Ugandan, Pakistani and Lebanese. Most recently, Mr. Speaker, Kitchener was fortunate enough to be able to welcome 1500 Indo-Chinese refugees who were brought over through the efforts of privately sponsored groups in the Kitchener area. These refugees have much in common with the German Mennonite settlers who arrived in the Kitchener area from Pennsylvania in 1800. As pioneers, they brought with them the technical skills and traditions of their homeland. They set in motion an intermingling of cultures and ideas that is still evolving 180 years later.
Mr. Speaker, the community spirit and sense of social concern, expressed in sponsoring the Indo-Chinese refugees is a recent example of the numerous and varied voluntary efforts and organizations that exist in Kitchener. Some of these are: the regional branches of the Canadian Cancer Society, the Canadian Heart Foundation, the Canadian Mental Health Association, the Rotary Club, the Kinsmen, the Knights of Columbus, and numerous other church and social organizations.
The multicultural centre provides a focal point through which the many ethnic groups of the area can enjoy each other's heritage. The Kitchener-Waterloo folk arts festival, which is an example of this, is being held this June and I am looking forward to attending.
The people of Kitchener, Mr. Speaker, are an open-minded citizenry. They are also very industrious and resourceful. From its austere beginnings with a few hundred settlers, Kitchener is now a thriving and prosperous industrial centre with a population of 135,000. There are 314 manufacturing plants and a total work force of 75,000. The female labour force is 45 per cent of the total, well above the national average. So as you
can see, Mr. Speaker, both men and women pull their weight in the economic enterprises of Kitchener.
Just as a footnote to that, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to be aware that the chances are better than average that on a daily basis the members of this House and the people of Canada own, use, or consume products manufactured in my riding. Some of the national industries located in Kitchener include Electrohome, BF Goodrich, Uniroyal, Schneiders, Greb Shoes, Krug Furniture and Budd Automotive.
Mr. Speaker, 1 should now like to focus more directly on the issues of national unity, the referendum and constitutional reform leading to a renewed federalism. As the member of Parliament for Kitchener, I feel very strongly about the mosaic that is Canada, and the different groups which over the years have made our country unique. The cultural mix of my riding spans virtually every corner of the globe. Interaction between French, English and other cultures makes us that much more complete as a people. However, Mr. Speaker, Canada is at a critical point in its history. Throughout the nation there are forces driving us apart, rather than bringing us together. In Atlantic Canada the promise of large oil reserves has led to controversy between the provinces and the federal government. In Ontario there are many who are fearful and resentful that the hold Ontario has exercised as the economic leader is slipping away.
In the west alienation in British Columbia has increased. In the prairie provinces, and particularly Alberta, there is talk in some quarters of separation. My unshakeable conviction is that the status quo, symbolized by the British North America Act, is no longer an option in Quebec and no longer an option in Ontario or in any of the provinces. The decision in favour of fundamental change has already been made, brought about by the dynamics of Quebec society since the "Quiet Revolution" of the 1960s, and crystallized in the results of the referendum vote on Tuesday.
The people of Quebec have stated that they wish to remain in Canada, but they do so based on certain assumptions about the rest of Canada. One of these assumptions is that the government and people in the rest of Canada recognize and understand the consensus in Quebec and that there must be fundamental alterations in the constitution.
A second assumption, Mr. Speaker, is that those of us who live outside Quebec will be willing to work with Quebeckers to build the structure of a new Canada, and more broadly, Mr. Speaker, that all Canadians, no matter in what region or province, will co-operate to build the structure of a new Canada.
A third assumption, Mr. Speaker, is that this constitutional reform will not be postponed indefinitely in a fog of words, procedural delays and competing priorities.
These assumptions indicate that the people in Quebec are reaching out in confidence and trust to the people in the rest of Canada. Thus, Mr. Speaker, you can understand why the response of English-speaking Canada to the federalist option of the beige paper is extremely important. Quebeckers have

May 22, 1980
taken a leap of faith by voting No, and voting Yes to Canada. They must be given the assurance that their own eagerness for change will not be met with sullen dedication to the status quo.
Constitution-making is never easy. It is usually impossible except as a result of pressures caused by war or revolution. Because of this, for the rest of us to give the necessary assurances to the people of Quebec also requires us to make a leap of faith-faith that Canadian moderation, good sense and willingness to compromise can lead to success. By giving these assurances, we commit ourselves to the difficult task of hammering out a new constitution. That constitution must reflect more completely the diversity and complexity of modern Canadian society. It must also be capable of handling the external challenges of a world in turmoil, as well as the internal social and economic pressures which Canada and Canadians will face in the years ahead.
Whatever the risks of acting boldly and decisively, the dangers to Canada of doing nothing are far greater. We must not succumb, Mr. Speaker, to lassitude and apathy merely because of the magnitude of the task and the failure to achieve consensus on important issues at past federal-provincial conferences.
1 say this for three reasons. First, 1 believe that we are nearing a pivotal period in Canadian history when the demands for change from Quebec will be met with a wave of dissatisfaction with the existing arrangements in other parts of the country. The impending clashes between Ottawa and Alberta this year, and probably later with Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, will certainly highlight serious constitutional and economic issues.
Second, the years ahead are years when unprecedented external geopolitical and economic pressures will make abundantly clear to all participants the indispensable role which the federal government must continue to play.
Third, the approach to constitutional reform in the 1980s will be to consider a package, rather than a piecemeal series of patches to the old arrangements. We will not be attempting to put new wine in old bottles. This should make possible hard negotiations as well as the accommodations and compromises which will be essential if success is to be achieved. We will not be starting cold. In fact, a great deal of work has already been done by various governments and interprovincial committees. Most provincial governments have published statements in favour of change.
In that the people of Quebec have taken the initial risks and committed themselves to Canada first, I believe it is appropriate, as a start to constitutional reform, to examine the issue from Quebec's perspective first as presented in Mr. Ryan's beige paper. This is a start, and obviously all provincial governments will be involved as will all the people of Canada. Constitutional reform will affect the daily lives of all Canadians and, as such, all Canadians must have a meaningful voice in its construction.
Constitutional Change
For years many Canadians have been asking, what does Quebec want? There could be no clearer statement than the one contained in the beige paper. This document is generous in spirit, civilized in tone, and is addressed to all Canadians. It recognizes the need for a strong central government. It invites comment from all Canadians.
The beige paper identifies 13 fundamental objectives, and then outlines a structure consistent with these goals. These objectives or principles form a key element in any future constitutional discussion. They should become familiar to all Canadians.
The first is to provide Canada with a constitution which is both modern and Canadian. The authors of the paper attach great importance to the symbolism of Canadians themselves- not the parliament of Great Britain-collectively and solemnly affirming the commitments and structures on which Canadian political life will be based in the years ahead.
Five principles are concerned with human rights. One involves a declaration of the equality of the two distinctive societies which give this country its unique place in the family of nations. This goal involves both linguistic rights and guarantees to Quebec which will enable it to maintain its unique personality despite the pressures arising from its position in North America.
This group of principles would also require the entrenchment in the constitution of the rights and liberties of individual Canadians. The fundamental rights of the first inhabitants of this country, the Indians and the Inuit, are specifically recognized, as are the preservation and development of the rich cultural heritages of the many multicultural groups of Canada. Equality of opportunity for all Canadians is emphasized, with a strong federal role in the redistribution of wealth to ensure the reality of this promise.
Two principles outline the commitment to the federal system. Two orders of government will continue, each sovereign in its area of jurisdiction. A specific pledge is made to guarantee the free circulation of individuals, goods and capital to all parts of the country, and a system of laws protecting the fundamental equality of all citizens. While an intergovernmental body is proposed to permit participation by the provinces in the government of federation, the beige paper explicitly states that the central government must be, and I quote:
-strong enough to serve the whole country in the face of whatever new challenges the modern world presents, whether internally or externally.
Five principles are concerned with the need for strong provinces, to ensure the development of their distinctive human and physical resources. The beige paper calls for clear definitions of the responsibilities of the two levels of government. Because Canada is so large and diverse, the beige paper opposes ad hoc extensions of federal powers and advocates a formal system for arbitrating constitutional disputes which clearly recognizes the duality and plurality of our population.
There is also need for explicit recognition of the provinces' role in international relations in areas under their jurisdiction within the framework of foreign policy.

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
Canada can never be a unitary state. Indeed, the forces at work in the last two decades have underlined its diversity and the need for a new approach which will underpin and build upon that diversity.
The beige paper provides all Canadians with an outline of a new federal system which accepts the fact that Canadians must find their unity in their diversity. It also defines the institutions and division of powers such a new federal system requires. Few will accept this outline in every detail. I do not. 1 think it should be questioned. Much sharp discussion and hard negotiation can be anticipated. In particular, finding a balance between decentralization and maintenance of an effective federal government will not be easy, but carried on in the spirit in which the beige paper was written, such negotiations give promise not of failure but of success.
Indeed, at a recent symposium held at York, Mr. Thomas Wells, the Conservative minister of intergovernmental affairs, accepted the 13 principles underlying the beige paper, declared that the Ontario government favours comprehensive constitutional changes, and stated:
We regard the Quebec Liberal party proposals as a reasonable and constructive basis on which to negotiate new constitutional arrangements for Canada.
The authors of the beige paper, as reasonable people, have addressed their thoughts and concerns to other Canadians. They ask us to recognize the problems which they see in our current constitutional arrangements and to undertake with them the great task of achieving change which will be acceptable to all, to achieve, in Mr. Wells' words, "a genuine national reconciliation."
In conclusion, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that achieving this without violence or bloodshed will further enhance Canada's reputation as a great country, a nation to be modelled after.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to intervene today with respect to the motion involving constitutional reform. I might say that undertaking constitutional reform involves something which takes a much longer time than not only a modest afternoon but indeed the next few years that have been allotted for it.
I hope I do not sound a note of pessimism-that is not my intention-if I suggest to you that I think the next few years are going to find constitutional reform important but probably of secondary nature. It seems to me that as we look at constitutional reform we will have to go through a much more fundamental process, and it is that fundamental process to which 1 would like to direct my remarks today.
I think part of the difficulty we have had over many years is the inability to understand who we are and where we would like to go. I have some considerable mistrust in constitutions. I have noted, and I am sure other members have, in the history of this century at any rate, that some of the most democratic constitutions, constitutions which had the most intensive language with respect to human, civil, cultural and linguistic rights, are those that exist in countries which have the most oppressive governments. I meant what I said and I hope it is not a note of pessimism.
The principles which the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) and others have mentioned must be based on something and I think they are based on certain realities, or ought to be based on certain realities about this country. I think there are probably some considerable difficulties for us, Mr. Speaker, as we attempt to determine what the fundamental realities of Canada are, because we have spent so long in making sure we don't know very much about the country. We have spent a long time and worked very hard in denying our own history, in, to put it another way, not paying enough attention, and in taking the country for granted.
I think the three fundamental realities of this country are going to dominate the next ten years and that is why I suggest that, over the next ten years, the idea of Canada, not the Constitution of Canada, is going to be the most important thing to address ourselves to.
Let me deal with the first of those realities as I see them, Mr. Speaker. I think that any stranger happening upon this land would come up with the first reality fairly easily. We are known best, and we know ourselves best, by our parts-by the parts of the country. Many speakers today have talked about regionalism. They have talked about their particular provinces, i think I could go from coast to coast and, like other members of this House who have had the opportunity to travel, I could take you to towns, cities, villages and neighbourhoods in Newfoundland right through to British Columbia, and in every one of those towns, cities, villages and neighbourhoods you will find the same instinct. People in St. John's, Newfoundland, think that that is the best place to live.

So, I could go from coast to coast, Mr. Speaker, and in each province, each city, town and village, and in each neighbourhood, the people know that that is the place to live. Regionalism in this country is a state of mind, one which is founded on geographical location, and it is rooted in an historical experience. That is why regionalism is so strong in this country. It is an historical experience and it is a geographical reality. That is why it is not an aggravation, why it is not a fly in another person's ointment. It is not an
May 22, 1980

imperfection because the regionalism from which we come, the towns, the cities, the villages and neighbourhoods-1 mention neighbourhoods only because in large cities one tends to identify with neighbourhoods-is real, authentic and necessary. It is from those areas that we get a sense of identity about who we are. It is in those areas where we have more control, in fact, over who we are and the ability to better ourselves and raise our children in value systems in which we can have a strong involvement.
The values which affect people most are those which come from small places. Countries other than ours which have large populations and small territory know the only way in which you can organize human nature is by having a strong value system and, as I say, that usually comes from small places. That is the first reality I see, Mr. Speaker, about this country. We are known by its parts and we have a regionalism which is enduring because it is authentic.
The second reality that I see is the opposite of the first. If regionalism is the first reality, then the second reality is the opposite of that. It takes the whole string of communities that the hon. member from Saskatchewan mentioned earlier, and binds them together. It is the opposite. Because the reality which organizes us best and determines that we are Canadians exists, I think, in the physical land itself. Most countries have something which defines them and tells them who they have been and who they are going to be. In some countries it is their art, in some countries it is the legislature, in some countries it is the military power, in some countries it may be the history, as in the United States, but in this country 1 think it is the physical aspect of the land itself.
I could take any member of this House on a boat, on a train, plane or bike, or we could walk it, to any part of this country. After they got off they would feel enormous pride about it. But they would feel something deeper. What they would feel, 1 think, is that the sense of Canada that they know is given to them from the land. Indeed, most of our historians have tried to explain to us-whether it is Lower or Creighton, Morton, Shortt, Harold Innis-that the fundamental reality of the country which takes us beyond our particular is the land itself.
This country in the past 20 years or so seems to have accepted the view that we are here in spite of geography and in spite of history. It is, indeed, the opposite. This country is here because of its geography and because of its history. I am reminded of the thesis, Mr. Speaker, of Harold Innis that this country takes on the configuration of the fur trade. All those towns and the building of each staple product as it came, exist because of geography and not in spite of it. It is interesting too, if you look at the lives of most of our historians. They had an intimate relationship with the land in personal terms. If you read Lower in his "Colony to Nation"-he was the most lyrical of our historians-his sense of the bush and his need to go canoeing, like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), is part of it. It is a sense of having to renew with the land. I don't think we should misunderstand what that means to us. It has animated every aspect of our life, not only our historians.
Constitutional Change
Take also the art which has endured. The Group of Seven and Tom Thomson in this country have endured because they reflected the land, and this is the message which comes from the paintings of the Group of Seven and from Tom Thomson. Interestingly enough there are no people in the art of the Group of Seven or of Tom Thomson, and there are no people in Donald Creighton's artistry with history in this country because they were reflecting the land. If you look at that art it is rugged, it has colour to it, and it is eternal. And that is where the strength comes from. I think that is also true of the music of this country. I do not know whether I should mention Gilles Vignault, but I think it is all right.

If you listen to his music you find that music tells you about the land. In 1962 when Monique Leyrac, as reported in the French press but not the English press, won an international award in Hungary singing Vignault songs, those three songs were about the land.
When Gordon Lightfoot sings, he sings about the Canadian railway trilogy. We know that is the land. For the maritimers present let me mention Stompin' Tom Connors. The best song Stompin' Tom Connors ever wrote was not about the mari-times but, indeed, about another town in Ontario. If you have ever picked tobacco, you know something about hard work, and he wrote a song called "Tillsonburg". "My back still aches when I hear that word".

I will leave that to the hon. member who follows me. I could use the squid-jiggin' ground. I have only 20 minutes; the hon. member can sing his own songs.
It is also true in sport. There are some people who think that hockey was invented, if not by Harold Ballard, then by Allan Eagleson. Hockey was not invented by either one of those people. It was invented by the frozen ponds in the land of this country. Maybe they should put some of the money back into it.
If you go down to New York to visit the United Nations building and look at all the flags of all the countries represented in that body, those flags represent either the history or the ideology, or both, of the countries they represent; all except one-ours. It is a leaf, and it reflects the land.
So the second reality in our constitution building is recognizing that the geography and the land and our response to that land will always be there. No matter what politicians and other people say, that is what unites us.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
The third reality which I would like to mention and one which I wish I could spend some time on, because we have spent so little time on it, is our traditions. 1 have been impressed with the desire on the part of all hon.

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
members of the House, and, indeed, all commentators, people interviewed on sidewalks, on television on radio and so forth, for a new constitution. Constitutions do not happen every two weeks. Every time we have a new thought, we do not build a new constitution. Constitutions are not merely a reflection of a particular generation. Constitutions reflect past generations and the values they engender, as well as current values, and as well as our hopes for future values, and 1 think it is that aspect that is worth mentioning. This third reality is the traditions of this country. They are good traditions; they are not bad traditions. Traditions are collective memories.
The licence plates of the province of Quebec used to say "La belle province". Now they say "je me souviens", "I remember". That is right; we should remember. The collective memories of this country are worth remembering as we build a new constitution.
This country has been a monarchy since Louis XIV. It is not fashionable to mention the monarchy, I think, but I do so because 1 was impressed some years ago when I read a book called "Freedom wears a Crown" by John Farthin. Farthin pointed out that the reality is not the royal family or whatever affection we have for the lady who is the Queen or the man who is the King at a particular time. The reality of the monarchy is the Crown, and from 1864 to 1867 in all of the discussions in the confederation debates the reason we did not have fundamental discussions about fundamental human rights and civil liberties of any significance or account was because they were assumed. They were built by generations, and the Crown reflects the civil liberties you have, Mr. Speaker, and that 1 have, and that my children will have. Whatever one wants to do in the future in this country with the monarchy, let us not confuse it with the significance of the Crown.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
1 was going to mention female athletes as another tradition-1928 was a good year for female athletes- but I will not get into that.
I think the most fundamental tradition in this country is one for which we are involved in no small enterprise because of the first reality of our particularisms. There are over 3,000 miles from one sea to another, and because of the second reality of the strength of the land itself, we are involved in what Parmenides wrote about. I hope 1 have that right. The Greek scholars here can correct me if I am wrong, but 1 read something by him which struck me. Parmenides said that the riddle mankind has-and it struck me that that is our riddle-is the riddle of the multiple and the One. He said:
Is the One alone real and the multiple merely illusion? Is the multiple alone real so that the world is irremediably and irreducibly pluralistic at its core? Is the world a gigantic process consisting in the unification of a multiplicity destined to be brought into a higher unity with the One?
That is pretty heavy stuff. Hon. members might want to read that tomorrow. Some may want to take it home to Hamilton, but in a sense most of us have been talking about that today because our contribution to the ancient Greek
riddle of the many and the One is the concept of federalism, and we do it better than anybody else in the world.
Canadians know more about it and have dealt with it longer than any other people. It has allowed us to have not just unity; it has allowed us to have more than unity. It has allowed us- not only the Europeans who came here but before the white man came here-to create. There were Indian confederacies. The federal principle has allowed us to take the first two realities and make them one, because what it has done is to allow that diversity and that unity to exist. That federal principle has guided us for centuries. We have had five constitutions under it, not one. There were constitutions in 1774, 1791, 1841, responsible government in 1849, and in 1867. We have amended the constitution on a number of occasions. That constitution and that federal principle have served us for a very long time. It has served us in good times and bad times and in war time and peace time.
That BN A Act is not a piece of paper that you chuck away.

It has allowed us to do what we want to do. We can make things smaller or larger. It is a house of many mansions. We need only to decide what we would like to do with it, and it will serve us again. The federal principle requires only two things. First, it requires tolerance, and not tolerance which is based on assuming that we are all brothers. The American understanding of tolerance is to make sure that they can deal with their similarities. The Canadian way has been the opposite, out of necessity. We have to understand toleration by celebrating the differences, and it is the celebration of those differences which is the glory of the country.
The second thing it requires other than toleration is the constant need-and 1 got into trouble once before, so I will make it clear-to talk, discuss, and negotiate, because negotiation and discussion are the mother's milk of the federal system. Those who would argue that we should draw lines are also the people who end up shooting.
The federal principle will continue to serve us, and we will be able to continue to solve the riddle of the many and the One, as long as we not only exercise toleration by making sure those differences are appreciated and celebrated but also make sure that we understand the necessity of discussion and negotiation.
Mr. Speaker, it has been a pleasure for me to have the opportunity to speak on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, we are presently living in a crucial period of the history of our country. The problems we will have to solve are difficult and complex. As members of this Parliament, we must uphold and promote together the values which unite us. Naturally we will
May 22, 1980

not always be in agreement but, as Brown, Macdonald and Cartier, we will have to find a new formula for today's Canada. This formula will have to take into account the fundamental needs of our society, including understanding, in order to meet the challenge of tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, that lets you know the extent of my use of both languages. 1 am going to keep trying, let me tell you.
I wanted to enter this debate today because 1 have given, like most hon. members, a lot of thought to the future of Canada. 1 have watched as the battle raged, rejoiced as the results became known, and felt both a sense of happiness and a sense of foreboding as 1 watched on television the final vote and the response to the recent referendum in the province of Quebec.
I think we must all be careful because something in excess of 40 per cent of the people of the province of Quebec said they did not like the way the country was going and they did not like the relationship between their province, the federal government, and the rest of Canada. As I watched that evening, it became clear to me that the one thing we must not think is that they were defeated, because there were no victories and there were no people who lost.
What happened in Quebec that day was that a number of people who wanted to see some fundamental change went to the polls and expressed two somewhat different views of how that change ought to take place. It is now our responsibility here in this Parliament, in all the legislative assemblies in the country, and yes, even in the municipal councils and across the electorate, to look seriously at what kind of change can be brought about that can satisfy the majority, that will lay the ground work, and that will establish the base from which Canada will grow into the future.
As I said in my few brief words in French, whatever French it may have been, we in this Parliament probably have the most difficult task because we must set aside our parochialisms, we must put aside the divisiveness which frequently creeps into many of our debates and which will, in one way or another, determine what shape the country will have in two, three or four years' time. We cannot all win on every point, and there will be necessity for give and take; there will be the necessity to recognize that not everything that everyone wants can be accomplished at one time. We have to take the lead in that regard. We in this Parliament have a job which will probably-I say this without overblowing our importance- parallel the very first Parliament of this country. It is an exciting time at which to be in the House of Commons, because the decisions that we make here over the course of the next few years will be the decisions that the people of Canada will live with through the next 50 years.
Whether or not we recognize the aspirations of the many parts of Canada, whether we put it into writing, whether we establish a constitution-no matter how we write it, no matter how carefully we try to incorporate everyone's desires and everyone's feelings-in the end what will matter most will be whether or not we will approach this task with good will,
Constitutional Change
whether we approach this task without the burden of having to take positions simply for the sake of being re-elected.
I worry when I look around the country because you can almost tell from experience over the last few years-and I have had the benefit, which others had, of having sat in a provincial parliament and of watching provincial politics as somewhat of a student-when we are about to have a provincial election, because slowly the words creep into the debate that it is the federal government's fault. It is called, as my colleague says, Ottawa bashing. It happens all across the country in every provincial Parliament. The unfortunate part is that it takes place a couple of months immediately prior to the election and it takes two or three years to resolve it, if ever at ail. It sets the mood that has people in British Columbia believe that someone in Quebec put the French on the cereal boxes, and it sets individual against individual. It makes people in other parts of the country believe that perhaps the problems that they encounter in their day to day lives are the will of someone else in Canada.
1 think that politicians will have to stop and take stock of what their role is to be. We will have to be much more serious about it. We cannot be frivolous about the future of this country. We cannot simply engage in debate for the sake of scoring some political points which may well undermine the confidence of the electorate. When I pick up the paper and read of the premiers of the provinces, I find that, without going into detail, one by one they stake out their position for the negotiations that must take place. If it is not resource rights, it is more autonomy; if it is not more autonomy, it is that Ottawa has not treated them well in the existing confederation. The problem with that is that, like everyone else, they are able, for one reason or another, to convince people who live in this country that these illusionary, imaginary things are real.
If you travel across the country and speak to the individuals in many communities, you find that they are not arguing, not blaming each other, that they are not blaming the people in Hamilton, in spite of the conflict between themselves and Vancouver over the football games that are played. Do not think that the people in British Columbia are undermining or in any way destroying their place in the Canadian society. Yet one might get the impression from time to time that the politicians who presume to speak on their behalf are trying to leave the impression that this is in fact what is happening. You find farmers in Alberta who are being blamed for oil price rises, strangely enough, by people in British Columbia. You find that the politicians in general are not responding in a less partisan way.
I want to suggest some things about this. First of all, I think it would be useful in this Parliament if we could clearly set out some time, over a period of years, when Parliament would be able to sit as we are doing today-maybe even with some people present-and talk about what our role as Parliament ought to be in the new confederation. There is no question that there will have to be a dramatic change in the formula which

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the process of constitutional reform has begun. For just a few hours this week Canada's newly elected Parliament understood and shared a common purpose. It is almost sad to realize that Rene Levesque's pledge to dismantle confederation was needed to prompt a little patriotism throughout Canada. Even so, like many others 1 savoured the results of the referendum in the hope that Canada will survive at least this century and beyond, if possible, intact.
Although the No vote must not lull English Canada into inaction, constitutional reform must not be seen as the cure-all. When was the last time the average Canadian read our constitution or, for that matter, the British North America Act? The cold fact is that a constitution can only provide a framework and not a sense of national purpose. A constitution guarantees a certain minimum standard of behaviour. It is important for all minorities-the French, the Italian, and many others-in that it provides guarantees. But this is only a base to build upon. I think a great many Canadians from every province would agree that the country's problems stem not from our constitution but, as I said, from our politicians. Every four years some provincial premier spends two months blaming every conceivable problem in the land on the federal government, and then they have an election. This is one problem that constitutional reform cannot resolve. It will require instead greater honesty among our politicians, and a more critical electorate.
A catch phrase that is making the rounds these days is the one about control of our resources. Western provinces, and now the eastern provinces, argue that given control of their oil and gas reserves harmony will follow. The real question is: who has control now? With a couple of exceptions like Petro-Canada and Saskatchewan Potash, most of our resources are controlled by foreign companies and not the Canadian government. If there is to be a transfer of control over oil and gas, it should be from Exxon to Petro-Canada.

Constitutional reform may be a start. National unity will come when it is understood that no matter where in Canada one is born, there is an equal chance to build a good life.
Canada's resources must be used to promote the stable growth of all parts of Canada. The oil and gas will eventually run out even in Alberta, and together we must prepare Alberta's economy for that day. At the same time we must allocate some of the oil and gas revenues to assist the underdeveloped regions in this country. The point is that federal guidance is necessary in order to smooth out the highs and lows in the economy. Whoever is given jurisdiction over Canada's resources must be able to see beyond provincial boundaries.
For the people of Ontario I want to say, on behalf of those I know, that they are eager to share with all others in the distribution of economic opportunity. If, over the years, as my smirking Conservative colleagues might think, others feel Ontario was less than understanding, I want to suggest very strongly that it was not the citizens of Ontario who were to blame. It may have been the government, but it probably was the very people who operated on Wall Street and Bay Street and who now operate on Jarvis Avenue in Edmonton-Jasper Avenue in Edmonton.

I should like to comment on the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) that Canada is land and frozen ponds. Canada is 23 million people. They are industrious, sensitive, generous and diverse. They are people who can and will rise to any challenge, who can and will realize a national dream. The only thing that stands in their way is the desire of politicians to use them for their own ends.
