subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate the opportunity I am given tonight of participating in this debate on the constitutional question. I am happy to see that the New Democratic Party decided to devote one of its allotted days to the constitution and that we should be invited to speak to a resolution inviting the House to interpret the referendum vote of Tuesday last as an unmistakable call for constitutional reform.
May 22, 1980

Mr. Speaker, 1 agree with the request that the House of Commons launch a constitutional reform. 1 have believed in the need for it for a long time and still believe in it. It is unfortunate-as the former speaker pointed out that, and if 1 recall his words correctly, he said, "It is ironic"-that the PQ party should have been the one to provoke us into proceeding with a reform of our constitution. That really does not bother me very much but, what is important, is that we should, as parliamentarians, as government, commit ourselves to changing the terms of our constitution.
Mr. Speaker, we undoubtedly need a new constitution in which will be enshrined basic and linguistic rights. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that, as far as the basic issue is concerned, it would be wise to say that we should set any deadline. We should expect that writing a new constitutional document, deciding on a new basic constitution is something that is going to take a lot of time, a lot of patience, a lot of energy. But there are certain things we should be able to do.
There is one thing that the referendum that took place in Quebec last Tuesday should enable us to do. There is now in Canada, as we saw in this House yesterday afternoon, a feeling of wanting to do something. Several of us said, particularly in the last three, four or five years, that we wanted a new constitution and in fact this government in June, 1978, brought forward a document entitled A Time for Action and a legislative measure that was referred to a special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on the constitution. We of the Liberal party have been committed to constitutional reform for a long time. We are happy today to see that because of what happened in Quebec, because the campaign of the No side also advocated change, Canadian parliamentarians, provincial premiers and, I imagine, provincial parliamentarians interpret that vote as a desire for change, and they are committing themselves to undertaking a constitutional reform.
Mr. Speaker, we must clearly understand that we must use the feeling that exists now but it can only do certain things because it is impossible to elaborate, to build-I am using words like "build"-a new constitution because it is more than a simple matter of writing a document. A constitution is more than just a legal and political document. A constitution must express a desire by all Canadians to live together, to build a better society, a society in which each and everyone will be respected.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, one thing we should be able to do is patriate the constitution. This we could do, thanks to the feeling we now share. Not because of some threat. We should never accept that anyone, either French or English-speaking, proceed with constitutional reforms under the threat of some deadline. We should do so because we want to. And patriating the constitution is one of the important elements of constitutional reform with which we want to proceed.
Constitutional Change
The second element is the amendment process and amending formula. In my view, this is the second important part in that debate. And I would say further that we should make sure that the feeling that is prevailing this week does not vanish before we reach that goal. But the third important part, after patriation and the amendment process the amendment formula and the constitutional reform process is the content itself. And there difficulties will arise. Let us not fool ourselves, let us have no illusion.
It will be difficult because trying to reconcile all the different interests in Canada will be hard and long work, but what is important, Mr. Speaker, is that we should repatriate our constitution, that we should make it into a Canadian document, and that both Houses of the Canadian Parliament, either by themselves or with the provinces, can work on constitutional reform. We should be able to agree before too long on an amendment formula and a process to bring it about.
As concerns the federal Parliament, one thing should be done urgently, and that is that, at least as concerns federal rights, we should pass legislation to entrench in the Canadian constitution basic individual rights and linguistic rights, and I did say legislation respecting federal rights, and this according to the principle of Bill C-60, so that when the provinces want to do the same for provincial rights, they will be able to do so.
However, what I am saying applies only to basic individual and linguistic rights and federal rights, because 1 respect the fact that some rights come under provincial jurisdiction. However, there should be a mechanism to allow the legislative assembly of a province anxious to entrench in its constitution certain fundamental and linguistic rights of provincial jurisdiction to do so. In the case of New Brunswick and Acadians, this would allow us to entrench in a new constitution or in the existing one certain fundamental and linguistic rights which are of federal jurisdiction, but also certain provincial rights, because since about 13 years, the former Robichaud government and the present Hatfield government have undertaken to entrench in the constitution certain linguistic and basic rights. Even if we did so only to help the Acadians, 1 believe it would be worth while because there are not very many Acadians as New Brunswick is not a very large province.
Mr. Speaker, if in a small province like New Brunswick with a relatively large group of Acadians, people are not able to agree on their political future, how can we expect to agree throughout Canada? It is not a matter of figures, a matter of quantity, but a matter of will. And if we in New Brunswick do not succeed in giving assurances to Acadians who want to protect their language and their culture, and in making Anglophones understand that it is good for New Brunswick, if we are not successful in that endeavour in a small province like ours, if we cannot express that will, how can we expect to express it throughout the country? Then, it is not a matter of figures, it is what might be called a moral issue, a matter of will.

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
Mr, Speaker, 1 say that we should commit ourselves to changing the constitution, to repatriate the constitution within a process of constitutional reform. As federal parliamentarians we should propose a legislation on basic rights and linguistic rights. 1 emphasize that we should not limit provincial rights. That mechanism would allow any province anxious to do so to enshrine in its statutes linguistic and basic rights whenever it decides to do so. And that would be important for the Acadian minority in New Brunswick.
With respect to the reform process, Mr. Speaker, 1 must say that in our previous approach-and 1 want to make here a positive criticism of my party's approach on that issue-in the past we always had intergovernmental negotiations. The constitutional negotiations that we have had since 1966 have for the most part involved governments only.
Mr. Speaker, we must see to it that something is added to that. Obviously, there is a need for negotiation between governments but in my view the importance that parliamentary assemblies, the federal Parliament and provincial legislatures may have in solving that problem should not be minimized. Provincial and federal assemblies should have a mechanism which could be semi-permanent. We should probably consider having a Canadian parliamentary assembly on the constitution, not a parliamentary assembly which would be empowered to decide on a new constitution, but between governments, there are sometimes close links with respect to civil servants or policies and it is possible that these might thwart the process.
But one should not minimize what elected parliamentarians might accomplish in a forum composed of a delegation from the Canadian Parliament, a delegation from the legislatures and the Canadian Senate. It could be interesting to see what the upshot of such discussions could be; these discussions could be held on a regular basis for one month, six weeks or two months a year somewhere in the country to decide not only on the need for a new constitution but also on the way in which this result could be achieved. And 1 must stress the fact that a parliamentary assembly should not make decisions but simply constitute a forum for discussions between elected representatives.
Mr. Speaker, i think such a process could do much in the way of helping to define various regional interests, cultural and economic interest within the country for parliamentarians can sometimes more readily understand one another's aspirations and this is what we must do in Canada. I myself, as an Acadian from New Brunswick, should be able to understand the aspirations of Canadians from British Columbia, Newfoundland, Quebec and Alberta. They in turn must also be in a position to understand those of the others. One thing that intergovernmental negotiations do not allow for is a true discussion of those aspirations. They are negotiations between governments which have close links with respect to their civil servants and their policies. One might say that when we have all those people in front of television cameras, it is a good place
to make what is known as set speeches, to put up an act, and that is important, it must be done. But, Mr. Speaker, I would like those questions to be debated outside that format, not exluding that format, but we could have another debating forum to discuss Canada's constitutional future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been one of the truly uplifting days of Parliament. This has been a tremendous debate. We have heard marvellous speeches. It is something from which we can all draw encouragement, the fact that we as members of a diverse House of Commons, coming from diverse parts of the country, can meet together in debate on the future of our country. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has done a great service to the House by introducing the motion which he has set down on the order paper. Indeed, I would like to congratulate the hon. member, not only for his motion, but for the speech which he made today.
We have heard outstanding contributions in this debate from the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) who made an outstanding contribution and set out the position on behalf of our party.
I suppose that 1 am in a unique position in terms of this debate or this resolution, a resolution with respect to the outcome of the momentous and historic Quebec referendum. I am one of the few members of this House who lived through a referendum, a privilege which I share with my colleagues from Newfoundland. Indeed, we lived through two referendums. In 1948, after some 15 years of direct colonial rule, Newfoundlanders, by referendum, were asked to vote on whether they wanted to continue that colonial type of administration which was administrated directly by civil servants from Westminster, or whether they wanted to revert to dominion status, which Newfoundland enjoyed prior to 1933 under the Statute of Westminster-which is the same statute that gave Canada its sovereignty-or whether we wanted to confederate with Canada.
I recall very well the trauma of that time. I can feel for what happened in Quebec. I can empathize with the people of Quebec in what they are going through right now in this post-referendum period. Indeed, we were encouraged, and I was certainly very pleased to see the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), following the decisive results of the referendum in Quebec, reach out a conciliatory hand to the minority in Quebec which felt strongly enough about sovereignty-association. They felt strongly enough about the independence of Quebec to go and cast their ballot for that question, in many cases alienating the affection of their relatives and friends by so doing.
That is important because I recall the post referendum period in Newfoundland. I recall very well the night of the second referendum. At the time I was working as an active
May 22, 1980

member of the Young Responsible Government League. 1 lived in a part of Newfoundland which was staunchly anticonfederate. My job as a member of the Young Responsible Government League was to be an agent in the polling booth. 1 did that during both referendums.
Of course there had to be a run-off because, on the first referendum, the outcome was indecisive. There was not a clear majority for either of the three questions. It is interesting that in the first referendum, independence, if you like, or sovereignty-association, if you like, responsible government as we knew it, won the day. But in the second referendum the confederate option won, because there was only two questions remaining. The two questions were whether to confederate with Canada or whether to continue to revert to dominion status.
I recall walking home that night to my house, Mr. Speaker, and looking at my father who was crying. That is how strong our feelings were running at the time. I remember the feeling on the street as 1 talked to my neighbours, and how strongly I felt as I passed our old parliament building. For some reason there were flood lights on it. I remember a lump coming in my throat because 1 felt the sudden realization that we would no longer exist as a separate entity. We had lost. We were the sovereign-associationists of our day and we had lost!
It took years for that feeling of bitterness to subside, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, you will still find it in Newfoundland today, and there are those who would take advantage of that feeling. They do so at their peril. That feeling still exist to a certain extent. I know it existed when I came here as a young member of Parliament in 1957 because the constituency that elected me then did so largely because of the anti-confederate sentiment that still existed. One of the ironies of the time was that we had no political parties, so the confederates joined with the government of the day and became the Liberal party, while the anti-confederates joined with the opposition of the day-hence I am a Progressive Conservative. There were no political parties, you see. Our constitution was in suspension. We had no legislature as it had been in suspension. Indeed, political parties were not permitted to exist save for those that were permitted to organize, as they were in Quebec, for the referendum.
1 remember coming here in 1957 with a certain feeling of bitterness still there-bitter because of the way it was brought about. We felt we had been short-changed. We felt that somehow the British government and the Canadian government had got together and decided that this would, in the long run, be best for us and that in insidious ways they were able to influence the outcome.
I did not realize until 1 came here, Mr. Speaker, the diversity and majesty of Canada. When I went to school 1 learned British history. We did not learn Canadian history. We learned very little about Canada, and the little we knew about Canada in the Newfoundland 1 grew up in we learned from the Canadian Armed Forces who were stationed overseas in Newfoundland during the war. Hence, I can speak with
Constitutional Change
some feeling of this country because I became a Canadian by way of referendum-1 suppose I am a statutory Canadian-a referendum that took place on July 22, 1948.
The constitution that we are now talking about patriating was amended on March 23, 1949, and royal assent was given at Westminster in order to make provision for Newfoundland's entry to confederation.
When I came here in 1957 what did 1 find? We were divided in this House on the question of whether we should have bilingual cheques. Can you imagine that-whether the French-speaking citizens of this country were to receive cheques from the federal government in their own language! Up to that time all government cheques went out in English only. This was a new dimension of Canada for me.
I recall that at that time a French Canadian could not stand in his place in this House and speak in the French language because, if he did, no one would understand him. Not only did the late right hon. member for Prince Albert bring in bilingual cheques, but one of the first things he did when he became prime minister was to provide the simultaneous interpretation that is in this House today.
This is not the Canada of 1949, Mr. Speaker. We have come a long way. This is not the Canada of 1957. An expression was articulated by my leader, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, when he said that Mr. Levesque and those associated with him wanted to separate from a Canada that no longer existed.
It is not for me to articulate the grievances of the Frenchspeaking people of this country, our brothers and sisters in the province of Quebec. I can speak of the grievances of my own province and I will.
Sir, what 1 want to say in the few minutes left at my disposal tonight is this: 1 believe in Canada. I am happy that the people of Quebec, by a democratic expression of their vote, demonstrated belief in Canada. I believe in strong provinces. I believe in strong provincial governments-provincial governments that have the constitutional authority to discharge their mandate, to carry out the obligations they have to their constituents, but I also believe in the absolute necessity of a strong federal government.

I look at the power grab taking place in this country today by some of our provincial premiers, and it shames me. 1 can stand in this House and articulate the views of my constituency; I have the responsibility of serving my constituency, and 1 have the concomitant responsibility of serving my province, but I have an equal responsibility in this House to serve my country.

That is why 1 reject those who would put forward the proposition that the Government of Canada can only enjoy those powers that the provinces delegate to them, that somehow the Government of Canada is perceived as merely the agent of the provincial governments. I reject that notion, Mr. Speaker. 1 reject it for many reasons, not the least of which is that it would create a Swiss type confederation in Canada, with a Government of Canada that had no power to serve its people to speak for Canada.
I hope, sir, as was so eloquently expressed today by my colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale, that in our pursuit of constitutional renewal we do not look on the British North America Act as a piece of paper and throw it out. It has served us well. It is one of the oldest constitutions in the world. We have been able to grow and prosper under that constitution. It is a constitution that could permit Bill 101 in Quebec. It could permit French Canadians to come to this House and find expression in their official language.
Let us not sit down with the attitude of carving up the pie. If we do that we will destroy Canada. Let us sit down and share in the dream that is Canada, a dream of the Fathers of Confederation. If we do that we will succeed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is almost superfluous for me to say, after all those who spoke earlier in this debate, that I join in the motion introduced by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). I congratulate him for his altruism and for that of his party, through him, because less than 48 hours after the results of the referendum became known in the House of Commons, he has enabled us to reaffirm solemnly the commitment made by the federalist forces to the people of Quebec that a negative vote on the question asked by the government of Quebec meant in fact a step on the road to change. It is for me symbolic that the dust having hardly settled on ballot boxes the House has already had the opportunity to hear the three national parties represented in this House state that it is very important for the survival of the country to devote the respite given to us to nation building, and I agree.
I was deeply interested by the speeches made by the hon. members for Provencher (Mr. Epp), Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) and the one made by the previous speaker, the member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I would like to say that I was deeply moved when, 30 years later, he referred to the heartbreaks induced by both referendums in that province and the fact that even after all those years, the people of that province still remember. I express the wish, Mr. Speaker, first that in 30 years from now we will still be in this House of Commons to say as Quebeckers: I remember the referendum in 1980 but
also I would like to say then: You know, I was on the No side at the time and 1 do not regret it since Quebec has taken its place in the Canadian federation, its rightful place, and that happened only a few months or a year or two after the people of Quebec stretched its hand out to the rest of Canada as it did the night before last.
1 am happy that the hon. member for Provencher took the opportunity tonight to draw attention to the regionalistic dimension of this desire for change. Let me explain. Everyone knows as well as 1 do, Mr. Speaker, that the Pepin-Robarts report gave a diagnosis of the situation, with which I agree, and said that there were two currents of change in Canada. One current, from Quebec, could be termed the nationalistic current, and the other, of which Alberta is perhaps at the moment the torchbearer, the regionalistic current.
I was glad that the hon. member spoke of this dimension because 1 think one of the biggest mistakes of the Quebec government was to presume and state that the other partners in confederation had no desire for change and that a No vote would simply allow all Canadian federalists to sit back and watch the world go by. But we realize now, and the hon. member has proved it, that this desire for change exists not only in Quebec but that it is echoed, and forcefully so, for perhaps differing reasons, in the regionalism of western Canada which is demanding adjustments to our constitution and institutions.
Finally, it is perhaps the hon. member for Rosedale who fascinated me most, because he indirectly opened a door which I myself wanted to open, and that is to warn all those who will be responsible for constitutional change, those who will bring it about, not to be lured by change for the sake of change.
Let me explain this. The hon. member said "You know, in the final analysis, the constitution of 1867 served us well." You will be surprised to hear that from a Quebecker; it is probably true. It would be sad to cross out our whole past for the sake of change and to feel obliged to build anew without putting to some use the experience that we have acquired and must preserve. 1 like very much the saying which has become very popular now, that instead of pulling the old house to the ground and building a new one, it is better to keep the nice architecture, the high wails and the large and aired rooms of the old one and to renovate them, to upgrade the insulation, to improve the heating system and to keep our link with the past which survives through the house and is beautiful.
You know, 1 have the feeling that if there ever was a myth that has been excessively used during the debate, it is the idea of status quo. Obviously, nobody wants the status quo. It has become the villain in Canadian politics. But is there only anything like status quo in Canadian constitutional law? 1 wonder and I am asking every hon. member. Not sure. Strictly speaking, the constitution of today is not that of 1867. It has changed and developed along with the times and needs, in line
May 22, 1980

with other legislation, the British North America Acts-there are a whole series of them-the Statute of Westminster, through constitutional amendments, both provincial and federal. The constitution of today, whether in the tax, monetary or power-sharing areas, is not that of 1867. One can rightfully say that we live today in a system which was conceived in 1867, but one could not say that the rules of the constitution under which we live today are those of the 1867 constitution. We are living under rules which have evolved. If these rules, therefore, have evolved, it is because the formula itself is not so bad after all, and this is one of the reasons-there are indeed others-why I believe in federalism. 1 believe in it and, until proven wrong, I shall continue to do so.
Alas!-and here I agree with the hon. member for Rose-dale-the problem we must face today is not, strictly speaking, a problem of constitutional reform. Of course the federal government, in March 1978, and before that, in October 1977, presented during federal-provincial conferences a whole series of proposals for constitutional reforms, on such esoteric matters as the declaratory power, the power to spend, natural resources or offshore rights on the continental shelf, which are all very important, of course, but which are all matters with which I am not sure that all Canadians can easily identify.
Reforms had therefore been suggested and the process was underway to make certain necessary adjustments, which leads me to say that we should beware of using the term status quo in Canadian constitutional law because it does not reflect reality. 1 do not believe that this is the real crisis; the real crisis is one of identity. And, as I said earlier, 1 would like to warn those who will bring about this reform against making simply a legalistic reform, a reform of the legal texts, against playing a political give and take game during these federal-provincial conferences mentioned earlier by my colleague from Gloucester (Mr. Breau) which could be compared to a circus where everyone is trying to gain some advantage so that when they go home, whether it be to Edmonton, to Quebec City or to St. John's, they will beableto mark political points. Unfortunately, this is just about what has happened in past constitutional conferences and even during federal-provincial conferences on energy or the economy, and we have to avoid falling in this trap.
Indeed, you can believe me, Mr. Speaker, even if 1 said earlier that the major issue may not be constitutional reform, but rather a change of attitude-and I shall unfortunately not have the time this evening to explain in detail what this change of attitude should entail-this change can have various manifestations, for instance, the creation of bilateral consultation mechanisms, a decentralization of decision-making, the creation of a House of Federation, a mechanism of shared membership among the provinces and the federal government, and so on. That could be discussed at length. But that has
Constitutional Change
nothing to do with the constitution as such; it is rather the institutions themselves that will have to adjust.
As 1 was saying, let us not kid ourselves, this is indeed the last chance that Canadians will have to reidentify with their country. The hon. member for Rosedale talked about the land, and I did like his image. For some it might be the land, for others, the sea, but the fact still remains that our crisis is one of identification. Mr. Speaker, if we cannot find a way to solve that crisis of identification, and very rapidly, I am afraid there will not be any need for a second referendum, and perhaps involving not only Quebec but other partners as well, for Canada as we know it now may no longer exist five years hence. It is the danger as I see it, the danger I apprehend and the reason once again why I would dare hope that that reform, that desire for change on the part of all Canadians will be expressed in two different ways. First, of course, to clean up that hotchpotch of necessary proposals for change, but that can sometimes blind us, make us think that here is the solution, the miracle solution is the spending power, the declaratory power, the offshore rights under the continental shelf, ownership, oil wealth. Some think solving that will solve the problem. No. But let us clean that up as rapidly as possible. Perhaps that can be done at the conference that will take place in July.
But that is not all. It would also be necessary, in a second step, that the conference in July be the starting point for that reflection and over-all reform that would finally enable us to better identify ourselves with our institutions. As I said, several proposals have been made, by the Pepin-Robarts commission, or in the beige paper of Mr. Ryan, by the Canada West Foundation or by the government of Ontario, in Bill C-60, or again by the Canadian Bar Association. Many groups have offered proposals, huge documents, reform proposals. There are many good ideas in there, proposals which may indeed help Canadians to better identify themselves with their institutions, which would allow a really dynamic federalism.
One solution could be to ask officials, and I would like this to be done on an intergovernmental basis, to collect and organize all this by the month of July-l am almost finished, Mr. Speaker, I need only 30 seconds more-so that we could, at the July conference, after having organized this hotchpotch, we could establish intergovernmental bodies to study these proposals and reach a consensus as soon as possible and, once again, on an intergovernmental basis. At a second stage, in maybe two years, we will reach proposals agreed on by consensus which could be submitted-one can dream about it-to a national referendum. Then all Canadians could vote on these proposals prepared by politicians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1, too, am quite moved and feel very privileged to partiepate in the debate on the motion. I was very moved by the speeches made

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
by hon. members earlier in the debate and 1 find my interests and concerns overlapping those of members in all parties.
I think we all have deep feeling and emotion and a love for this country. Some of us have been deeply troubled as we have moved out of the decade of the seventies. My hon. friend from Rosedale spoke with soul and feeling. He is obviously a man who understands his community, his region and his country, as do the speakers who followed him. 1 was touched to hear my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), give his experience, stating the fact that he is a statutory Canadian in that he joined this chamber and this country as a result of a referendum. We heard that Canada today is an idea, not a constitution, that historians and artists reflect the strength, the beauty, and the magnificence of the land.
My background, my education, my reading, my work, my life, my region of the land, are quite different from those of members who preceded me, and I would like to place perhaps another broad dimension into the debate here today. Canada has come through a decade in which 1 have been troubled, as have others, in seeing the spirit of Canadian nationalism diminished. 1 have often related this denationalization to the social engineers working under the direction and perhaps with the assent of the government which was in power through the seventies.
I, like many Canadians from my region of Canada, carry a deep concern, yes, a resentment at the deterioration in the nationalism I was brought up in. I have seen this deterioration take place in the schools of my land when they stand to sing the national anthem. 1 have seen it deteriorate at the hockey and football games of my land as we sing the national anthem. Many of us are concerned that the spirit and the values which built this great country are diminishing. That spirit and those values carried our forefathers, my father and myself, through two world wars in my family, defending freedom and dignity for men, freedom of speech, freedom of ideas, freedom of movement, freedom of enterprise in a free marketplace, freedom to set individual goals and work to achieve them, all within a sense of order necessary to serve and protect the common weal and the common good.
We know that the racial crisis that we are in the midst of in this land has roots deep in the history of the nations of our French and British forefathers. But in spite of this historical antagonism, Canada came together as a nation with a constitution surely for some very fundamental reasons in addition to the land that we have heard of today, the love, the idea, and the referendum.
In May of 1979, a year ago, 1 received from a constituent an article in the Washington Post. It was written by John Conway, a Vancouver person, a scholar who moved to the United States as a lecturer in law and history. His article was written as an interested Canadian observer looking at Canada and what was happening to it from outside the land, not involved in the day to day work of it. The article was entitled "Canada is Coming Apart". In the files of clippings and literature which I have gathered, and which most of us have
gathered on this issue, that article stood out in that it expressed something I fully did not know from my knowledge of history and my schooling. He pointed out that Canada came into existence for three reasons resting upon a genuine distrust of the American democracy, founded on life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, as opposed to British constitutionalism.
He pointed out that Canada in its beginnings was afraid of American annexation. Indeed, he reminded us that in 1896 Theodore Roosevelt even talked of declaring war on Britain to conquer Canada, its resources and its land. The Quebec French Catholics did not like the idea of being forcibly etched to the bosom of the Protestant American Union. This was one of the feelings that was in the origins of Canada. English Canada, on the other hand, was founded by some 35,000 loyalists who had backed the defeated side in the revolutionary wars of the United States and had settled along the shores of Lake Ontario. They feared the Americans and disliked their political and social institutions. Concern about American annexation lasted in this country into the twentieth century.
The second reason Conway gave for confederation was economic. If British North America was to be united and strong against American attack, it must have a strong, stable, expanding and mixed economy. This led to tariffs to support founding industries in Canada, in Ontario and Quebec against American competition.
From the very beginning of Canada this policy was a source of irritation to the farmers on the Canadian prairies and to the harvesters of the natural resources on the west coast of Canada in British Columbia.
In British Columbia we have always had to compete in world markets with products from our resources. Our export dependence far outweighs that of Ontario and Quebec. In addition, we have had a slender hold on secondary manufacturing and processing of resources which are important to stable payrolls and long-term growth in those regions. This means that national policies have a very different impact on my part of Canada from that on other regions like Ontario and Quebec.
Canadian tariffs and quota restrictions are seen as a negative drain on our payrolls and on consumers and higher prices for consumers in all of Canada, while the benefits go largely into central Canada. I do not put this out antagonistically; I just seek understanding of that attitude which prevails. Antidumping Tribunal decisions which disturb western payrolls and industries and which transfer the market advantage to Ontario are indeed dangerous policies within the delicate nationhood we have.
The third reason he pointed out for confederation was the growing might of the British Empire. Canadians could not compete with the might of the industrialized forces of the United States, so British preferential trade agreements were in our history a great boon to us and were a great offset against a very powerful neighbour to the south. British preferential
May 22, 1980

tariffs are now being phased out, as three quarters of our trade is with the United States.
These three founding reasons have faded. We are intimately related to the United States economy in that 74 per cent or 75 per cent of our trade is now with the United States. The United States has no intention of taking us over through the force of arms. We know that, although its influence and economic power over us are a challenge which we must recognize and face. The British Empire has faded like all previous empires. It appears, therefore, that of the founding reasons for our nation only one in part remains, and that as a nation we are searching and looking for the base upon which to reconstitute ourselves.
Although anti-Americanism is raised from time to time in Canada, so far it is only the product of the intellectuals. I do not see the rank and file average Canadian perceiving it as an issue. Even in British Columbia we are concerned about the extent of Japanese economic domination over our resources and over the secondary industries adding to the value of those resources. Could it be that in addition to the land the only other rationale for reconstituting our nationhood lies in more self-determination and control over our resources?
We in British Columbia want to see initiatives on two fronts, the economic front and the constitutional front, where amendment is necessary. We are impatient with a struggle and a structuring to concentrate power to the centre. We want to see a federalism based on co-operation and with guarantees for inputs from the regions of this great country. Most of us in the west believe that the problem is economic, and would like to see a healthy economic environment exist in order to resolve the cultural and language problems which are within our bosom.
At the moment we have an impatience with the posturing for duality of language, law, and culture. It will take a great deal of talk, such as we have had in the meeting of minds, hearts and feelings in this House today, to create the understanding needed for duality of language and an at home feeling from sea to sea to come about in this country. 1 believe there are federal powers, as my predecessors have said, which must be strengthened, and that a strong central government is absolutely necessary for this country in order for it to take its rightful place in the community of nations. But to do so by the central government's grabbing the resources of the regions is indeed a strain on the threads which tie and bind us together.
Quebec has been the first to speak out. The west feels that its frustrations, although of different origins, are equally valid. Conway writes that without the empire, without the unifying ideology, and without the charter myth such as the Declaration of Independence, we are retreating into regionalism and indifference. I think May 20 snapped us out of indifference. Now we in this chamber have to talk our way out of regionalism.
He also challenged that all three political parties in Canada have failed to address these fundamental issues upon which the survival of our country depends.
Constitutional Change
In closing, let me echo the words of my colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). The present constitution really needs two things. It needs tolerance-"Let us celebrate our differences"-and talk. This chamber needs heart-to-heart talk. We have lost ourselves in closed caucuses which do not allow us to express in this House the sense of regionalism that we were elected to bring to the federal government. That debate started back in Britain in the late 1700s, and I think we in all parties have to address it today.
I should be able to stand up and talk to hon. gentlemen across the way and to my left and my colleagues here openly, in front of the media and the Hansard of Canada, and express the feelings and the emotions of my home in my part of Canada. 1 should not have to be locked into a caucus of silence when I do so. Without talk how are we ever going to understand each other and defeat the regionalism which has descended upon us? 1 believe the challenge before us lies in this chamber today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to do something a little bit odd this evening by finishing off the address I started on the seventh day of the throne speech debate. You may remember that you were in the chair and that I had the last ten minutes, and tonight 1 have a bit more time. I think it is timely, since 1 was talking about the protection of minority language rights and minority rights in general, that I finish off that part of my speech and talk a little bit more about what 1 think has to happen in terms of constitutional change from the perspective or vantage point of an Ontario member of Parliament.

But first, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat part of a speech 1 made before this House some four years ago. 1 said at that time that many English-speaking Canadians born in Canada forget all too easily the fate that a minority group must suffer. Just ask a newly arrived immigrant in Toronto if it is easy to be accepted by the majority. The answer, 1 reckon, will be a loud no.
New Canadians must face difficulties because of their linguistic and cultural differences. They must face discrimination because of the colour of their skin or their religion. Immigrants generally accept these difficulties. They consider them as the price tag of their acceptance in this country, Canada. The same is not true of French-speaking Canadians. They represent more than a minority, Mr. Speaker, they are part of a minority with has a status of equal partner in the Canadian nation-state.
In my opinion the Official Languages Act is a wonderful thing and contributes to the unity of this country. It spells out the legal right of Canadians of both official languages to be served in their respective language by the national government throughout the country.
1334

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
Where it is feasible, I think that the people want the government to establish this service. But now, Mr. Speaker, we must go further, especially after the results of Tuesday's referendum in the province of Quebec. We must entrench linguistic rights in a new Canadian constitution.
1 would say, Mr. Speaker, that one of the main reasons that 1 wanted to come back to this House, as I mentioned the other night, was to see a new constitution, and to see minority language rights enshrined in that constitution. 1 applaud the speeches of some of the premiers of this country, such as Mr. Davis, Mr. Hatfield, and even Mr. Lougheed, who are prepared to enshrine minority language rights in the constitution. That may help to win the hearts of those in Quebec who really delivered for us the other evening when they voted overwhelmingly No to sovereignty-association for the province of Quebec.
But there are other aspects of the constitutional debate that have to be analysed. As a member of the House from Ontario I think that Ontario has to make many sacrifices if the other regions in this country are to feel at ease with being part of the continued Canadian confederation. I want to talk for a moment about resources because resources are to western Canada what language and cultural rights are to Quebec.
I am glad that the premier of my province has made a public commitment to enshrine minority language rights in the constitution of this country. But I also think that the premier of my province and his government, the members of the provincial legislature and the members of parliament from Ontario, have to recognize the legitimate aspirations of those people from western Canada with respect to resource management and ownership.
I would agree with some of the comments made by Premier Blakeney when he said in Toronto recently that one cannot talk about federal taxation on revenues flowing from oil and natural gas if one is not prepared to apply the principle across the country no matter what the resource. I think the people of Ontario will have to realize that they cannot expect the western provinces, in particular Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, which have most of the oil and natural gas in this country, to accept a lower price, to accept federal taxation of that resource, unless resources in the province of Ontario are equally taxed.
1 have a couple of things in mind here, Mr. Speaker. Uranium is a great export from the province of Ontario and, to my knowledge-and I stand to be corrected-there is not on it the same kind of export tax, if indeed any, that applies to the export of oil and natural gas. With regard to hydroelectricity or electric power, I saw some figures this afternoon when I was signing a question which will be produced in the House in a few days from the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) about the sale of hydroelectric resource to the United States. It is my understanding that electric power in general, when exported to the United States, is not subject to the same kind of tax that we have levied on exports of oil and gas to the
United States. So, to use that old adage-and I hate to use it-what is good for the goose is good for the gander, I think for too long people in Ontario have lived comfortably and have perhaps behaved a little like ostriches, not willing to recognize the legitimate aspirations of other parts of the country.
It is my hope to see in this debate what was so eloquently expressed this evening by my colleagues on all sides and I took particular delight in the comments made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) who, in my view, united themselves with most, if not all, members of the House in the desire to hatch up regional differences, to maintain a strong, united country but also to maintain a federal power and the national Parliament which has the ability to protect all people across this country, whether it is to protect minority language rights, English in Quebec, French outside of Quebec, or whether it is to protect the federal power in setting national standards in certain programs which we have accepted in the last 20 or 30 years as the right of every Canadian. One that comes to my mind is medicare. I would say quite frankly that one of the worst things I did when I was a member in the Thirtieth Parliament was to vote for a piece of legislation which, en bloc, had the effect of transferring the powers over medicare to the provinces.

We need a strong national government to maintain a good medicare system and equal access to medicare. We need a strong national government to ensure that all the resources of the country, whether it is oil in the west, or uranium and hydroelectricity in Ontario, are shared equally across the country. All the resources, such as off-shore fishing on the east and west coasts, belong to all Canadians, and it is only with a strong federal power and a strong national government that these resources will be shared equally among Canadians.
We need a strong national government to ensure the freedom of movement of goods, labour, and capital across provincial boundaries. I think that what the hon. member for St. John's East said a few moments ago struck the core of the problem. In the last few years this basic principle has been seriously eroded. I think that some of the talk about decentralization, about the devolution of power and the need to weaken the central authority, is really a figment in the imagination of certain bureaucratic and political elites in this country. That is not to say that we in this chamber and our public service here in Ottawa are also not an elite that wants to protect its own sphere of interest, but I think that if we are really going to solve all of our problems we have to look beyond our petty interests, whether those interests are the ones I have described, the political and bureaucratic elites federally or provincially, or whether they are the petty concerns of people in their
May 22, 1980

respective provinces. We have to agree to put these aside, and we have to agree to unite and all make sacrifices.
The vote the other night was great for us from English Canada. We appreciate no end the decision taken by the majority of people in the province of Quebec; but the heat is now on the rest of us from outside of Quebec not to break the faith of those people who voted in Quebec. So we must push for constitutional change, and 1 hope that the good wishes expressed in the House in the last couple of days will not dissipate as the referendum results move farther away from us.
I think we reali7.e-and I believe this sincerely-that we have very few years left to make sure that this country stays together. The problems in this country, whether they be language rights, the legitimate recognition of the economic aspirations of the provinces or the sharing of wealth in this country, must be attended to. We must in this Parliament, as 1 said the other night, pledge ourselves to come forward with a new constitutional document.
I was quite glad to hear the response of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the question from the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) in terms of participation of the member for Oshawa and of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in any federal negotiating team.
We have had two elections in the past year. They have left a bitter taste with some members, not just those of the former government. I might remind hon. members that I was one who paid the supreme sacrifice last May, and then came back. It has been a tough year, but politics and our political fighting in election campaigns are what make this country democratic. As indeed the Prime Minister said about the referendum, where else but in Canada could one part of the country legitimately debate openly the future of that part of the country and put it to a democratic vote? We are a very mature country.
Since two elections are past us, and since the referendum is past us, we in this House can bicker back and forth about specific programs. Perhaps I should not say "bicker", as we all have legitimate differences. But on constitutional matters I really hope in a most sincere way that we will put our differences aside. Whether it is an all-party federal negotiating team with the provinces, or whether it is some other kind of mechanism, 1 hope we can all submerge our differences and agree that we must make some sacrifice. It will not be easy.
It will not be easy for someone like me to go back to metropolitan Toronto and tell people that higher oil and gas prices must be levied or must be gained by the western provinces, and that growth must shift further west. It will not be easy for me. It will not be easy for the hon. member for St. John's East if he has to go back to Newfoundland and say to the people of Newfoundland, "You cannot claim all of the jurisdiction over offshore mineral rights". Those are some of the sacrifices we as members will be called upon to make in the next few years. I hope all of us are equal to the task.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 too am very grateful to be here in the Parliament of Canada on this occasion, on the occasion of talking about the referendum in Quebec, on the occasion of talking about constitutional renewal for Canada. 1 think it is the politicians who have not yet recognized that Quebec is different. 1 think it is some politicians, anyway, who have not yet accepted this marvellous duality that is Canada. speechtext:
There will be lots of important discussions- one just needs to read the beige paper, for example-on the courts and their composition, as well as the fascinating subcommittee of the council, that is proposed to deal with dualis-tic matters. But the big one will be the division of powers, and we all know that.
We have heard a lot of talk in this very fascinating debate today about whether or not we can have a reasonably strong federal government particularly in the area of economic development, or whether we will have a society where all economic development matters are left in the hands of the provinces. It is interesting to observe that over the last decade or so it has been the provinces that have been taking the initiative in economic matters.
It was never true in the past that the provinces took very many initiatives, certainly not in social and economic matters. But in the last decade or so-in fact some people would say since the Second World War-the federal government has been on a continental drift. There has been no Canadian economic development policy. Some people would say that there has not been any since Sir John A. Macdonald. But even looking at the last dozen years, there has not been a national economic development policy. The only major development at all was the establishment of Petro-Canada.
How do we know whether we as a people, we as members of provinces, we as citizens of different parts of the county, want to have a strong federal government, particularly in economic matters, when we have allowed the role of the federal government to drift totally over at least a decade? In other words, we not only have to address constitutional reallocation but, indeed, even before we make decisions on that, we have to decide as a people whether we want to see the federal Government of Canada in co-operation with the provinces have a Canadian economic development policy. It is crucial, to me, that we make that decision.
I was very moved, as I think we all were, by the speech of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). As he was speaking I was wondering whether he and the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) had ever engaged in a friendly debate because, as I understood the hon. member for St. John's East, he was saying that one of the marvellous things about being a Canadian is that you can feel a part of
every part of this country no matter where you live and no matter where you come from-you can feel it.
I have heard lots of people in British Columbia say, when they were afraid that Quebec might separate, "Quebec belongs to me too". We do have this feeling, or many of us, about every part. I have it for New Brunswick because of my father's background, about Ontario because of my education, and about B.C. because that is where I live. I have it about other parts of Canada too. I think everyone has it even though they may never have left home.
The hon. member for Rosedale was saying that he thought a fundamental reality of this country was regionalism, a state of mind rooted in historical experience. With all due respect, 1 think that day is over. One of the fundamental facts of this generation in this country is mobility-we move around.
I am practically a senior-I won't use that phrase; I am practically an old timer in British Columbia. I have been there six years but most of the people I meet there now have only been there two. The big feature of Canada is its mobility. I agree with the hon. member that there was a period when all of our paintings, particularly the Group of Seven, were only of landscapes. That is not true any more; we are a society of people. There was a period when we stayed home and never moved; that is not true any more. We move right across this country. We move and we must encourage, through government action, more young people to move backward and forward across the country.
1 have only one more theme I particularly want to address. Two or three hon. members have referred to the suggestion that more than governments be involved in the constitutional negotiations. Or course, not being in a government, I think that is a splendid idea. We have to look at the way it might be done. It was suggested by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) that it might take place after the first ministers' conference; that there might be a sort of constituent assembly after that first ministers' conference. 1 think my leader's suggestion was that the actual delegations at the first ministers' conference should have a multipartisan make-up both from provincial and federal spheres, and that there should be at least leaders of other parties in the delegation. At this time of, I hope, a joyful renewal in Canada I think that would be an act of magnanimity, but more than that, an act that has a chance of real success. The delegations would have to do a lot of talking among themselves first, but it would have a chance of real success to have the federal delegation multipartisan, and the provincial delegations the same. I would hope, therefore, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would take that into consideration very seriously.
The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) had an interesting suggestion as well. His was more a way to involve more members of Parliament in a forum of discussion; it would not be more than a forum of discussion, but to mix them up with members from the provincial legislatures. I think that is an additional means of furthering our understanding of one another and, therefore, deserves to be thought about seriously,
May 22, 1980

in this case by us as members of Parliament with our counterparts in the provincial legislatures.
1 for one look forward to the real opportunities that the referendum and its results have given us all as Canadians. I think they have taught us a great deal, as I said earlier, and when both the Yes and the No votes can be construed and are being construed as strong requests for constitutional renewal, we can approach the task not in a spirit, at least 1 hope not, of narrow regionalism. I do not think Canadians feel that way any more. 1 think we can approach it in a spirit of wanting to create through the kinds of policies, particularly in the economic sphere, that this country has been crying for for years- a new Canada. Thank you.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe in Canada; 1 believe in Canada with the passion of a convert, like so many other new Canadians who have come to this country and who have chosen to become Canadians because of their faith, their hope, and their observations of the greatness of this land. 1 hardly need to dilate upon the greatness of this nation after the eloquent tributes that have been paid verbally today and the last day or so, and certainly 1 hardly need to expand upon it after the tributes that have been preferred, not only in this House, but, above all, by the votes that have been cast by the people of Canada in the province of Quebec, expressing their faith in the most excellent way, far greater than words could ever state, when they voted in the referendum, choosing for Canada.
Given this background 1 want to say that I will not trespass upon the tributes given to Canada, either by those who have spoken so eloquently in the House, or by those who have voted so eloquently in Quebec. However, 1 want to state that I believe in Canada as one who has become a Canadian, like so many others who become Canadians and who have come to this country, as I did in 1951, and in years before and after, people who have come with a faith and a belief, and have come to appreciate what Canada can do for them, and what a great and free land it is. 1 believe in this nation as those new Canadians do.
Perhaps I have that kind of concern that comes not just out of reason, that comes from those who have perhaps always lived here and look at their country with great satisfaction, but with something that comes from experience.
1 was born in Switzerland and I lived in France just before the Second World War began. My father was the Protestant chaplain general of the French army. He saw that that nation, as 1 saw it, was, if you will, complacent; complacent with what it had, complacent with the way things were and, in fact, unwilling to make any changes that would adjust and permit it to face up to the world that was changing about it. My father paid with his life for his efforts to try to awaken France to the dangers of the complacency in that country. And so, perhaps, out of that experience as a child, seeing what could happen to what is called a great democracy, 1 saw also how great was the price that was paid. As Georges Santayana said, and as the words are immortalized on the gates of the prison at Dachau,
Constitutional Change
"Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it."
It seems to me, therefore, that one has to say as a Canadian who was not born here, one has a love for this country that is the love of a convert. From having experiences and seeing what happened in other nations, one knows what a great country this is and one wants to be sure it does not happen here. Perhaps it was for this reason that 1 attended conferences in 1971 in an attempt to convince people of the need for dialogue among Canadians, to talk about what was separating us, what was making us different, and what would bring us back together again in a sense of sharing, understanding and cooperation. Perhaps it was for this reason, 1 would suggest, that 1 entered the political arena, to participate in this great dialogue which now, once again, is beginning in great earnest in this country.
Why? Not because of rational reasons, but because of experiential ones. And those who have not learned from the past are bound to repeat the mistakes of the past. Those of us who do not learn from the past of Canada are bound and doomed to repeat the mistakes that have been made in the past in Canada.
I believe that we are faced with two choices. On the one hand, we can enter once again into the trivial argumentation of constitutional haggling of small points and of fine points the unsuccessful route that we have followed until now, or perhaps we might take a bolder approach, and 1 suggest we do that.
A bolder approach would be to enter into a faith in a new country, to undertake a rebirth in this nation that would bring about a new Canada on this continent. In other words, we must look to transcend and overcome the past rather than to bicker about whether or not this belongs to me and that belongs to you. As we focus on what belongs to me and to you, we lose the vision of what belongs to all of us. This rebirth of a nation can come about in three ways. They are essential if this nation is really to come into a new life.
The first thing, 1 think, is to fight the threat from within. The only way a new nation comes into being is the same way, in fact, that some people in Quebec wanted their new nation to come into being, by fighting what people regard and perceive as injustices. If we intend to fight the enemy from within, we must correct the injustices of the past and present with a completely new approach, an open heart, and an openness toward one another. We must have the enthusiasm, the idealism of a population that wants to right wrong, obtain justice for all, and that perhaps has the same kind of inspiration which fired the separatist cause. We need a new spirit within, a moral appeal and a moral renewal.
The second way, I suggest, is by combating the external threats, by protecting our air space from pollution, by protecting our land from pollution, our offshore resources in the 200-mile limit, our fishing rights and our internal channels of communication in the north which some may wish to say are our international channels. We must waken and realize that we are being threatened from without, not by armies but by a

May 22, 1980
Constitutional Change
new form of danger, a new form of threat that can destroy us-pollution and destruction of our resources and the wasting of our country.
The third thing which we could do is to take pride in our country. This subject has already been mentioned, but it bears repeating. One does not create a new nation by trying to argue over what belongs to me and what belongs to you, but by grasping the vision and pride in this country of what we have achieved in the past and what we may be called upon to achieve in the future. We might be called upon to fight disasters, to increase our peace-keeping forces, to continue our work with refugees. We must continue to be concerned about the human rights of people in other nations.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we are shortsighted because we have gotten used to it. We are shortsighted when we look at only our own concerns in this nation, instead of looking beyond and realizing that the world is being torn apart by tyranny, nationalism and regionalism. One need only look at countries such as Cypress and Lebanon, at countries like France with its problems in Corsica, and Britain which is being torn apart through Ireland and Wales with their nationalism, and even the Scottish nationalism-all of which was once the United Kingdom. We can look throughout the world and see one nation after another being torn apart by civil war. There are countries like Bangladesh and Ethiopia. The tragic list goes on and on.
Do we really think in this nation that we are immune from these forces which are tearing other nations apart, from the terrorism and violence which exists? If Canadians were to take the view of persons coming to this country from another country, if they could each step apart and aside and have the view of new Canadians, they would see this country for its totality. They have not become identified with its parts, and Canadians, too, would realize how important it is that we be united in a common cause.
We must look at the dangers that are without and come to appreciate the values which we have. It is only then that we can do, for example, what France was unable to do, to realize that the external threats and the threats of injustices from within will tear us apart like other nations, unless there is a renewal from within. We must renew our moral faith and develop a concept of a rebirth of goals, of our inner selves, each as an individual. It must begin with me, Mr. Speaker, and with you.
The problem will not be solved in this House. But the spirit that now prevades this House, of talking to one another, of really listening and not trying to find fault in the other, to see if we can hear something wrong in order to attack, and instead really trying to understand what the other person is trying to say, and helping that individual put it in the best possible light, that, Mr. Speaker, is dialogue. That is what will hold this country together.
I appreciate the rare privilege this evening of standing in the House of Commons. Though I was born in another land, I was permitted to adopt this land and I have had the good fortune of being able to stand in this House to speak on behalf of my riding and the many people in it who were either born Canadians or who came to Canada. I can say for them that we are grateful for what has happened in the last few days. I am grateful for the privilege of being able to add my few words of hope for a new country with a new start.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps fitting that I should be speaking at the tail end of this debate, because we in the north have been for so many years the tail end of the country. We are about to embark upon discussions with respect to the amending of the constitution of our country. I now make an appeal to be heard on behalf of Canadians who live above the sixtieth parallel.
The common southern conception stops at the sixtieth parallel, and the realization is not there that there are thousands of Canadians who live in Canada's two northern territories which comprise 60 per cent of our land mass. We have been treated by the government of the day as colonists. We have been defined judicially as colonists. 1 cannot help but compare that status with the progress that is being made throughout the world in the new nations which are emerging and which have a good deal less to offer to the development of a country than Canada's north.
The voice of northern Canada must be heard. It is represented in this House by three members, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar), the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), and myself. With the advent of party politics in the Yukon, we now have a government leader who is very able to speak on behalf of our concerns. In the Northwest Territories that development is taking place quite rapidly and their elected representatives should also be heard.
It was notable yesterday when we listened to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) that no reference was made to the participation in any forthcoming talks with respect to the reform of our constitution of the elected representatives of the north. The former prime minister, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) did make that reference-a reference which he seldom neglects to make when he speaks of the country as a whole.
The system which exists vis-a-vis the administration of northern Canada is archaic, to say the least, and repressive, to say the most. When we have elected representatives who must be present at the kind of federal-provincial conferences at whatever level through a minister who happens to come from Hamilton at the moment, this is simply not acceptable. It is no more acceptable than if I were to have the presumption to suggest that I could speak better for the residents of Hamilton and the riding which he represents.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-QUEBEC REFERENDUM RESULT-CALL FOR CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Particularly that one. As suggested by the former prime minister, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition
May 22, 1980

in his remarks yesterday, it is time to recognize that those Canadians living above the 60th parallel should participate fully in any conferences that are going to affect their lives as Canadians.
It seems to me the time is long past that we should be operating under a system which was discarded from 1879 onward. Since that date when Manitoba became a province at the insistence of the territorial movement of that time, there has been no further movement toward recognition, with full participation, of Canadians who are classified as territorials. Indeed, that classification puts us within the definition of what 1 believe to be second-class Canadians.
We have made some progress in the 1970s and a good deal of progress in the last year toward achieving some measure of determination which at least equates that of a municipal council in most parts of the country. We have a long way to
go-
My pitch-so that it is not misunderstood-is not for immediate provincial status, but for a relinquishment of the Liberal philosophy of maintaining a stranglehold on the legitimate aspirations of northern Canadians to make decisions for themselves which their own municipal administrations, like provincial administrations, have the ability to make now. It is a simple question of fairness.
There are many thousands of Canadians in northern Canada, including many thousands of native Canadians, who want that kind of representation in any constitutional talks with respect to the reformation that is about to be conducted. That desire has been made known to the government opposite,
I know, as it was to ours. Under the responsibility of the immediate former minister of Indian affairs and northern development, a good deal of progress was made toward achieving that equality which northerners have a right to expect in any democratic society.
The government leader in the Yukon has already communicated his desire to participate on behalf of the people of my territory-his willingness to participate in any constitutional reform talks that come up. While the Council of the Northwest Territories has not progressed to that stage in their development that we have in the Yukon, they too have elected representatives.
The time is long past, and I hope this course is not adopted by the government when it comes to the talks-I will not call them federal-provincial talks because they should not be that; they should involve a much broader representation than that- the time is long past when participants in those talks must be confronted with a fait accompli designed in the bowels of the Langevin Building. The time is long past when the talks must commence on the basis of a structured plan presented to those participating. The time has come when there must be a realization that the elected representatives of the people in the broadest possible sense, must be the designers of any reform that is to come about in our constitution-a constitution which, incidentally, has served us well, as has been pointed out by many previous speakers, particularly from this side.

It has served us well. The fathers of the BNA Act had remarkable foresight in designing a constitution which at the time was applicable to four provinces-Upper and Lower Canada and the two maritime provinces that participated. In 113 years we have progressed to the point where it needs updating but, as the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) said, it certainly does not deserve to be chucked out on the crest of the impetus we achieved on May 20.
My appeal tonight is that for the first time northern Canadians should be represented by their elected representatives, not by the bureaucrats in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and not by any other bureaucrats at the table. I do not suggest they be full participants on an equal level with provincial premiers but I suggest that the elected representatives of the northern territories, those Canadians who live above the 60th parallel, should be heard in person.
