subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-HEALTH AND SAFETY MEASURES TO PROTECT URANIUM MINERS
LABOUR CONDITIONS-HEALTH AND SAFETY MEASURES TO PROTECT URANIUM MINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, on April 30, I put a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) and asked him how soon the government would

May 22, 1980
Adjournment Debate
be moving to implement regulations relating to uranium miners concerning their health and safety. The minister indicated at that time that he hoped by May 30 there would be new regulations put in place to ensure the safety and health of the uranium mine workers in this country, especially in the province of Ontario so that they would be on an equal basis with those workers under provincial jurisdiction in other mining camps.
During the last several months there has been increasing concern that those uranium mine workers are working under a much less safe arrangement regarding health and safety regulations than those working under provincial jurisdictions. In fact, last August regulations were passed under part IX of the Ontario mining act, which has since become out of date because Ontario has moved on to Bill 70, the occupational health and safety act, which provides more up-to-date arrangements.
A few weeks ago we had a meeting attended by representatives of the United Steelworkers, and the Minister of Labour, the minister of mines and other representatives from the two operating mines in Elliot Lake to urge upon the minister that action be taken on this matter. At that time the minister gave an understanding or a commitment that he would look into a number of items, including a request that the whole question of the health and safety of uranium miners be put under provincial jurisdiction. It is very appropriate that this matter should be raised tonight when we have been talking today about the constitution and new arrangements between the federal and provincial governments, because the United Steelworkers of America believe that conventional occupational health and safety should be under provincial jurisdiction.
Also at that meeting the minister indicated that he would move to see if Bill 70, the provincial regulations bill, could be, by reference, appended to section 4 of the federal labour standards code. At the same time he indicated that he would review the decision of the former minister of labour authorizing the health and safety committees in those two mining operations in Elliot Lake. He has already moved to do that and I am pleased to see that that is under way.
I am concerned about the labour unrest that has resulted and the uncertainty there has been during the past few months, that he moves to reference these occupational health and safety regulations under Ontario's bill 70 and put them in place as federal regulations under the federal labour standards code so that we do not have two classes of miners in Ontario, but instead that we have them all operating with equivalent health and safety provisions. If the minister does this by the end of this month 1 am sure there will be great appreciation for that decision, certainly by myself and by the thousands of uranium mine workers employed in the Elliot Lake mining camp.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilbert Parent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Sports)
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-HEALTH AND SAFETY MEASURES TO PROTECT URANIUM MINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I compliment the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) for having brought up this important
question regarding the uranium miners in his riding, one which also affects all the uranium miners in Canada.
If I may, I will give a little of the background to put the subject into perspective before referring, in closing, to a decision which has been forthcoming from my minister.
Labour Canada's involvement in the uranium industry began with a legal opinion by the Department of Justice in October, 1978, that part IV of the Canada Labour Code applied to conventional occupational safety and health in uranium mines. Prior to that time, all aspects of occupational safety and health in the uranium industry were regulated by the Atomic Energy Control Board. This was accomplished by a clause in the AECB licence which required the companies to comply with all local, municipal and provincial laws. By this means, the provincial legislation in relation to mine safety applied to the Ontario uranium mines and was enforced by inspectors of the Ontario Ministry of Labour.
Subsequent to the legal opinion in 1978, the uranium mining situation was given top priority and immediate action was taken by the department to ensure the provision of services in the field of conventional safety and health. The hon. member drew attention to this in his own words.
At a January, 1979, meeting attended by representatives of the mining companies, the labour unions, Atomic Energy Control Board, Labour Canada and the Ontario Ministry of Labour, it was agreed that the existing provincial laws would continue to apply and be enforced by the provincial inspectors. This interim arrangement pertaining to the legislative requirements was formalized when federal regulations, which referenced the Ontario legislation, were proclaimed in August, 1979. At that time, however, it was recognized that new Ontario legislation would be in effect shortly and departmental officials planned to amend the federal legislation to reference these revised Ontario mining regulations. This approach was unacceptable to the union, which requested that the federal regulation be revised in a format that included the safety and health requirements in a detailed, clause-by-clause manner. Although departmental officials recognized that this would be very time consuming, it was agreed to proceed on this basis with a target timing for completion of late spring, 1980.
To resolve the conflicts that have arisen in the tripartite application of safety and health standards in the uranium mining industry of Ontario, it is proposed to place a submission before cabinet in the near future which would offer several alternative courses of action in the federal jurisdiction.
I hope this will be done at an early date so that the hon. member might soon convey to his constituents the decision taken at that time.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-STUDIES ON EMPLOYMENT STRATEGIES FOR WOMEN
STATUS OF WOMEN-STUDIES ON EMPLOYMENT STRATEGIES FOR WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am raising the question of a women's employment strategy this evening because the situation facing women in terms of high unemployment, cutbacks in support services, and growing poverty, is reaching crisis proportions.
What are the facts? First, unemployment among women remains persistently higher than that for men, close to 9 per cent.
Second, women still earn only 58 per cent of men's wages, and according to Dr. Ratna Ray of the women's bureau of the Department of Labour, the gap is widening steadily.
Third, women's employment counselling and training programs funded under Outreach have dwindled away under Liberal and Conservative governments to the point where there are fewer than 12 left.
Fourth, job ghettoization is worse than ever with 71 per cent of women workers still concentrated in the sales, service, clerical and nursing occupations.

May 22, 1980
Adjournment Debate
Fifth, technological change is placing jobs for women in even greater jeopardy and closing the doors to better paying and more interesting job opportunities.
Sixth, private sector corporations are succeeding in keeping women out of skilled trades and in hampering women's efforts to organize into labour unions.
While the situation facing women has deteriorated rapidly in the last decade, particularly in the last three years, both Liberal and Conservative governments have produced nothing more than vague promises, regressive cutbacks, and more rounds of studies. The decision by the current minister responsible for the status of women to carry out yet another study on a women's employment strategy with the assistance of Liberal vice-president Lorna Marsden, is of deep concern to me, for several reasons.
First, women have been promised an employment strategy many times during the last three Parliaments; by the former Liberal minister in March, 1979, by the former Conservative minister in November, 1979, and now by the current minister responsible for the status of women. The urgency of the situation requires the immediate implementation of job-creation and job-training programs for women.
Second, can the women of Canada look forward to action from a government that refuses to implement standards of equality among its own employees? The recent investigation of equal pay in the federal public service, and the growing number of complaints before the Human Rights Commission from women public servants suffering discriminatory wages, demonstrate that this government's commitment to equal pay for work of equal value and to job promotion for women is dubious. New programs and new standards in the public service are not necessarily needed. Rather, what is missing is the will to enforce existing programs and to demand departmental accountability. If enforcement is lacking in the public service, is it possible to expect this government to enforce affirmative action, job training and equal pay in the private sector?
Another concern is that this government and the minister responsible for the status of women have neither talked in terms of, nor made proposals for, a full employment policy such that everyone willing and able to work is able to find useful, rewarding, and decent jobs. In fact the opposite is characteristic of the Liberal government. Instead of publicly advocating that employment opportunities should be available for all women who want to or need to work, this government has helped to perpetuate the myths that women are secondary wage-earners, are the cause of high unemployment, are temporary aberrations in the labour force, and tend to abuse unemployment insurance benefits.
If the Liberal government has not yet adopted a full employment policy and has failed to develop a job-creation strategy, can we really expect a meaningful and serious employment strategy for women?
Finally, I question the need for yet another study on employment for women in view of the tremendous number of studies
and recommendations that have already taken place. They include, one, a study of women returning to the work force by the Advisory Council in April, 1979; two, six major studies costing thousands of dollars prepared by the minister's own department outlining the elements of affirmative action and methods for implementing such a program; three, a report by the National Council of Welfare on Women and Poverty in October, 1979; four, an employment strategy for women by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women presented to cabinet in March, 1978; five, another employment strategy by the National Action Committee presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on February 22, 1979; six, specific employment related proposals presented to the former Liberal minister in a letter dated March 23, 1979, from Yvette Rousseau, then head of the Advisory Council; seven, a brief by the Canadian Committee on Learning Opportunities for Women presented to the government on May 14, 1979; eight, "An Employment Service for Women", a paper done on contract for Status of Women Canada in July, 1979; nine, Towards Equality for Women, the Liberal government's own national plan of action presented in March, 1979; ten, a complete strategy for women's employment prepared by officials in the minister's own department, approved by the previous minister in the Conservative government and destined for cabinet consideration in December, 1979.
The last thing the new minister should need is more studies. [Translation]

The hon. member over-simplifies the situation of women in the work force when she suggests that implementation of all the government's previous studies should be undertaken immediately.
Implementation of such studies is impossible without some co-ordination and the assistance the department requires from those who act as consultants, co-ordinating past studies with present realities and policies. The employment situation of women is well known.

None of this work can be done overnight, nor can it be done without a co-ordinated and comprehensive strategy, one that is well planned and well thought out. This will be the first of a series of annual reports to be made between now and 1985, the period covered by "Towards Equality".
